The truly poor do not beg; Allah hates idle talk, wasted wealth and much asking; the Prophet gave some lest they fall into Hell; cutting firewood beats begging.
On the Tabuk expedition the Prophet estimated a garden's yield at ten wasqs, foretold a strong wind, received gifts from Aila's king, and praised Uhud and the Ansar.
A tenth is due on rain-watered land, a twentieth on well-watered land, none below five wasqs; the Prophet took a charity date from Al-Hasan's or Al-Husain's mouth.
The Prophet forbade selling fruit before it ripens and is safe from blight.
Umar was told not to buy back a horse he gave in charity; the Prophet's family eat no charity, but charity given to Barira became their gift.
Mu'adh was sent to call the People of the Scripture to Allah, prayer and Zakat, sparing their best property and fearing the oppressed's curse; the Prophet blessed those bringing alms.
An Israelite debtor who found no boat sent a thousand dinars to his creditor in a log thrown into the sea, and the creditor found it on sawing the wood.
No compensation is due for one killed by an animal, a well or a mine, but a fifth is due on Rikaz; the Prophet checked his Zakat collector's accounts.
Uraina men given the Zakat camels' milk and urine killed the shepherd and drove off the camels; caught, they had hands and feet cut and eyes branded.
Bringing a newborn for Tahnik, Anas found the Prophet branding the Zakat camels.
Zakat-ul-Fitr: one Sa' of dates, barley, raisins or other food for every Muslim, free, slave, young or old, before the Eid prayer; later people substituted half a Sa' of wheat.
At the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet let a Khath'am woman perform the obligatory Hajj for her old father, who could not sit a mount, and turned Al-Fadl's face from her.
The Prophet began saying Labbaik at Dhul-Hulaifa once his mount stood up carrying him.
The Prophet and Anas made Hajj on a packsaddle and Aisha rode one to Umrah; after faith and jihad Hajj Mabrur is best, women's best jihad, wiping away sins.
The Prophet fixed Qarn for the people of Najd, Dhul-Hulaifa for Medina and Al-Juhfa for Sham as the places to assume Ihram.
Yemenis came for Hajj without provisions, saying they relied on Allah, and begged in Medina, so Allah revealed that they should take provision, the best provision being fear of Allah.
The Prophet fixed Dhul-Hulaifa, Al-Juhfa, Qarn and Yalamlam as Miqat for Medina, Sham, Najd, Yemen and passers-by, those within assuming Ihram at home; Umar added Dhatu-Irq.
The Prophet prayed at Dhul-Hulaifa, went by Ash-Shajara and returned by Muarras, and was told Al-Aqiq is a blessed valley for prayer and Ihram of Hajj and Umrah.
Perfume before and during ihram, the Prophet's matted hair, his assuming ihram at the mosque of Dhul-Hulaifa, and the garments a muhrim may not wear.
The Talbiya: its words, begun when the Prophet's mount stood up after praying at Dhul-Hulaifa, said aloud, kept up until stoning Jamrat al-Aqaba, and the Prophet picturing Moses reciting it.
In the Prophet's last Hajj, those with a sacrificial animal kept ihram until Hajj ended and others left it after Umrah; Ali and Abu Musa took his intention.
Hajj-at-Tamattu and Qiran: Ali kept to them despite Uthman, pre-Islamic people shunned Umrah in Hajj months, and those without a sacrificial animal left ihram, owing sacrifice or fasting.
The Prophet spent the night at Dhi-Tuwa and bathed before entering Mecca, entering from its higher side at Kada' and leaving from its lower side.
The Prophet carried stones for the Ka'bah; Quraysh rebuilt it short of Abraham's foundations, which he would have restored but for his people's recent ignorance, and Ibn Az-Zubair later did.
Mecca is Allah's sanctuary; Aqil and Talib, not Ja'far and Ali, inherited Abu Talib's property; the Prophet would stay at Khaif Bani Kinana, where Quraysh had pledged against Bani Hashim.
An Ethiopian will demolish the Ka'bah, Hajj to it outlasts Gog and Magog, its cover and treasure, Umar kissing the Black Stone, and the Prophet praying or saying Takbir inside.
Ramal in the first three rounds, begun to show the pagans strength, and touching or kissing only the Black Stone and Yemeni corners, or pointing at the Corner when riding.
On reaching Mecca the Prophet made ablution and began with Tawaf; women circled apart from men, the sick rode, a man's leading rope was cut, and naked Tawaf was banned.
After seven rounds, two rak'at at Maqam Ibrahim, then Safa and Marwa, with no marital relations before that; Tawaf after the morning prayer, avoiding forbidden times, and circling while riding.
Al-Abbas could stay in Mecca on the nights of Mina to water the pilgrims; the Prophet drank Zamzam, praised those drawing it, and Jibril washed his chest with it.
Those combining Hajj and Umrah, like the Prophet and Ibn Umar, began with Tawaf of the Ka'bah and did a single Tawaf between Safa and Marwa for both.
Going between Safa and Marwa may not be left: Aisha and Anas explain the verse calling them Allah's symbols, the Prophet ran there, and relations wait until it is done.
A menstruating woman performs every Hajj rite except Tawaf of the Ka'bah until she is clean, as Aisha did; menstruating women attend Arafat but keep away from the prayer place.
The Prophet prayed the noon and afternoon prayers at Mina on the day of Tarwiya, and he, Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman early on prayed two rak'at at Mina.
On the day of Arafat the Prophet was seen not fasting, pilgrims said Talbiya or Takbir, set out at midday after a short sermon, and the Hums were sent there.
Leaving Arafat at a calm pace, the Prophet made light ablution at a pass, saying the prayer lay ahead, then joined the sunset and night prayers at Muzdalifah.
The weak and women could leave Muzdalifah by night; the Prophet prayed Fajr there at first dawn, left before sunrise unlike the pagans, and said Talbiya until stoning Jamrat al-Aqaba.
The sacrifice owed for Tamattu, a camel, cow or sheep or else fasting; riding one's sacrificial camel; and the Prophet and Ibn Umar driving sacrificial animals for Hajj with Umrah.

Garlanding and marking sacrificial animals, Aisha twisting their garlands, the Prophet sending them, sheep included, from Medina without entering ihram, riding a sacrificial camel, and giving their skins in charity.
Slaughtering at the Prophet's place at Mina, camels standing, cows for his wives, meat, skins and covers given in charity, none as butcher's wages, and keeping meat past three days.
Day of Nahr rites: no harm in changing their order, ihram kept until the sacrifice, the Prophet praying for those who shave before those who shorten, and Tawaf al-Ifada.
Asked at Mina on the Day of Nahr about shaving, slaughtering or stoning done out of order, the Prophet told each questioner: do it now, there is no harm.
The Day of Nahr sermon: blood, property and honour are as sacred as that day, month and town; the present must tell the absent; do not strike one another's necks.
Those watering the pilgrims could spend Mina's nights in Mecca; the pillars are stoned after midday, from the valley's middle, seven pebbles with Takbir, supplicating after the first two.
Aisha perfumed the Prophet before Tawaf al-Ifada; pilgrims make Tawaf their last act before leaving Mecca, menstruating women excused, and the Prophet circled after resting at Al-Muhassab.
A woman whose menses begin after Tawaf al-Ifada may leave without waiting, as the Prophet allowed Safiya; Um Sulaim's report backs Ibn Abbas's ruling, and Aisha performs Umrah from Tan'im.
On leaving Mina the Prophet prayed and slept at Al-Muhassab, a camping place rather than a rite, and Ibn Umar spent the night at Dhi-Tuwa on entering and leaving Mecca.
Muslims avoided trading at the old markets of Dhul-Majaz and Ukaz until a verse allowed seeking their Lord's bounty during Hajj.
Safiya, menstruating on the night of departure, was allowed to leave because she had done Tawaf al-Ifada, and Aisha performed Umrah from Tan'im.
Umrah expiates the sins since the last one; Umrah before Hajj is no harm; the Prophet's four Umrahs, none in Rajab and mostly in Dhul-Qa'da; Umrah in Ramadan equals Hajj.
Aisha, menstruating, left her Umrah for Hajj and later did Umrah from Tan'im with her brother; Umrah before Hajj is allowed for ever, its reward matching its cost and hardship.
Umrah rites as in Hajj: removing perfume, Tawaf of the Ka'bah and between Safa and Marwa, which may not be left, no relations before then, after which ihram ends.
On journeys: Takbir on high ground when returning from Hajj, Umrah or a campaign, not reaching home at night, hastening home, entering houses by doors, and joining prayers when hurrying.
A pilgrim prevented from the Ka'bah slaughters the sacrifice, shaves and leaves ihram, as the Prophet did when Quraysh barred him at Hudaybiyyah, and as Ibn Umar intended.
Troubled by lice at Hudaybiyyah, Ka'b bin Ujra was told to shave and fast three days, feed six poor people or slaughter a sheep; the verse came about him.
Whoever performs Hajj without sexual relations or sin returns as sinless as a newborn child.
Muhrims may eat game hunted by Abu Qatada, not in ihram, if none prompted or pointed it out; the Prophet returned a gifted onager since he was in ihram.
A muhrim may kill five harmful animals, crow, kite, mouse, scorpion and rabid dog, even in the sanctuary; a snake at Mina was ordered killed, and the salamander called bad.
Allah made Mecca a sanctuary: no bloodshed, cutting trees, chasing game or taking lost things except to announce them; fighting there was allowed the Prophet for hours of one day.
At Mecca's conquest the Prophet said emigration had ended but jihad and intention remain, and declared Mecca a sanctuary whose plants, game and lost things are protected, except idhkhir.
The Prophet was cupped and married in Ihram; a pilgrim may wash his head but not wear shirt, trousers or perfume, using khuffs, or trousers, if without sandals or waist-sheet.
In Ihram for Umrah, the Prophet was admitted to Mecca only with sheathed arms; he fixed where people of Medina, Najd and Yemen assume Ihram for Hajj and Umrah.
The Prophet entered Mecca in the year of its conquest wearing a helmet, and ordered Ibn Khatal killed though he was holding the covering of the Ka'bah.
A man came in a perfumed cloak; the Prophet received revelation, then told him to do in his Umrah as he does in his Hajj.
A man bit another man's hand, the bitten man broke the biter's incisor in the process, and the Prophet forgave him.
A man in Ihram whose mount broke his neck at Arafat is washed with water and Sidr, shrouded in two cloths, unperfumed and head uncovered, to be raised reciting Talbiya.
The Prophet let a woman perform Hajj for her dead mother, as one pays a debt, and a Khath'am woman for her father, too old to sit on a mount.
The Prophet sent Ibn Abbas from Muzdalifah to Mina at night; newly adult, he rode past the first row there; As-Sa'ib made Hajj with the Prophet aged seven.
Umar let the Prophet's wives make Hajj; Hajj is women's best jihad; women travel only with a mahram; a woman who missed Hajj was told to make Umrah in Ramadan.
Those who vowed to walk to the Ka'bah were told to ride: Allah does not need an old man's self-torment, and a woman should walk and also ride.
Medina is a sanctuary between its two mountains, its trees and game protected and innovators cursed; the Prophet built his mosque, called it Tabah, and said it expels bad people.
People will leave Medina though it is better for them; faith returns to it like a snake to its hole, its plotters dissolve, and afflictions will fall among its houses.
Angels guard Medina from plague and the Dajjal; it will shake out disbelievers and hypocrites; outside it the Dajjal will kill and revive a believer, but cannot repeat it.
Medina expels bad people as fire cleans iron, the Prophet said when a bedouin asked to cancel his pledge and when believers split over hypocrites who turned back from Uhud.
The Prophet asked double Mecca's blessings for Medina, hastened on seeing its walls, kept Bani Salama at home, and said a garden of Paradise lies between his house and pulpit.
When Abu Bakr and Bilal caught Medina's fever, the Prophet prayed Medina be loved like Mecca or more and its fever moved away; Umar asked for martyrdom and death there.
Ramadan's fast is compulsory with the five prayers and zakat; Ashura, fasted by Quraysh before Islam, became optional once Ramadan was prescribed; fasting is a shield that Allah Himself rewards.
Hudhaifa said prayer, fasting and charity expiate one's trials, but afflictions spreading like sea waves lie behind a closed gate that will be broken, and Umar knew its meaning.
The fasting enter Paradise by the gate Ar-Raiyan; in Ramadan Paradise opens, Hell closes and devils are chained; fasting follows the crescent, and fasting Ramadan in faith forgives past sins.
The Prophet was most generous in Ramadan when Gabriel met him; Allah has no need of a liar's fast; fasting is a shield; those unable to marry should fast.
Fasting starts and ends with the crescent, Sha'ban completed to thirty days if cloudy; a month has twenty-nine or thirty days: the Prophet's month away from his wives lasted twenty-nine.
None should fast a day or two before Ramadan; verses allowed relations on fasting nights and eating until dawn's white thread, so suhur may last until Ibn Um Maktum's adhan.
The Prophet forbade others his continuous fasting, urged suhur for its blessing, and on Ashura had it announced that whoever had eaten should eat no more but fast.
The Prophet sometimes woke in janaba and fasted after bathing, and kissed and embraced his wives while fasting; whoever eats or drinks forgetfully completes his fast, for Allah fed him.
Uthman washed his hands, mouth, nose, face, arms and feet as the Prophet did, who promised forgiveness of past sins to one praying two undistracted rak'at after such ablution.
A man who had intercourse with his wife while fasting could not free a slave, fast two months or feed sixty poor, so fed his family dates given for expiation.
The Prophet was cupped while fasting and while in Ihram, and Anas said cupping a fasting person was disliked only if it weakened him.
On journeys the Prophet let people fast or not, broke his Ramadan fast going to Mecca, and seeing a faster being shaded, said fasting on a journey is not righteousness.
Ibn Umar said feeding the poor instead of fasting was cancelled; Aisha made up missed days in Sha'ban; menstruating women do not fast; guardians fast the dead's missed days.
The fast ends at sunset as night comes from the east, as the Prophet showed on a journey; people stay on the right path while they hasten to break fast.
The Prophet had the Ansar told to complete the Ashura fast; afterwards they fasted it with their boys, giving those crying for food wool toys until fast-breaking.
Out of mercy the Prophet forbade Al-Wisal, fasting continuously without breaking at night, saying his Lord feeds him; when people persisted he fasted on with them until the crescent appeared.
Salman made Abu Darda break his fast, as Lord, soul and family have rights, and the Prophet agreed; the Prophet fasted and left off by turns, most in Sha'ban.
Abdullah bin Amr, who fasted daily and prayed all night, was told body, wife and guest have rights: fast three days a month, or at most David's alternate days.
Abu Huraira was advised to fast three days monthly; fasting, the Prophet declined Um Sulaim's food and prayed for Anas; a man who missed month-end fasts should fast two days.
The Prophet forbade fasting a Friday alone, chose no special fasting days according to Aisha, and drank milk publicly at Arafat when people disputed whether he was fasting.
Fasting on both Eid days is forbidden, Ibn Umar citing the ban beside the duty to keep vows; on Tashriq days only pilgrims unable to afford a sacrifice may fast.
Ashura, fasted by Quraysh before Islam and by Jews as Moses did, was ordered by the Prophet, then left optional once Ramadan was prescribed; he favoured no day's fast more.
Praying Ramadan nights in faith forgives past sins; Umar gathered the people behind one reciter; the Prophet stopped leading them lest it be made compulsory, and prayed eleven rak'at.
Praying on the Night of Qadr forgives past sins; it is sought in odd nights of Ramadan's last ten, its date withheld over a quarrel; the Prophet strove hard then.
The Prophet kept I'tikaf in Ramadan's last ten days, his wives after him; Aisha combed his hair from her room during menses; Umar was told to fulfil his I'tikaf vow.
Seeing his wives' tents, the Prophet left I'tikaf until Shawwal; walking Safiya home, he told two Ansari men Satan runs in people like blood; a wife kept I'tikaf while bleeding.
The Prophet's dream of prostrating in mud came true in I'tikaf; he had his wives' tents removed; Umar fulfilled his vow; the Prophet kept twenty days the year he died.
Abu Huraira narrates more than emigrants busy trading or Ansar busy with property because he stayed with the Prophet, and after spreading his garment at his word forgot nothing.
Abdur-Rahman bin Auf declined his Ansari brother's offer of half his wealth, traded in the Qainuqa market and married; trade at pre-Islamic markets in the Hajj season was allowed.
Between clear lawful and unlawful lie doubts: the Prophet was wary of a claimed foster marriage, doubtful game and stray dates, but doubt breaks no ablution and forbids no meat.
People left Friday prayer for a caravan; a time will come when none cares if money is lawful; exchange is allowed hand to hand; Umar missed a ruling while trading.
A wife giving household food in charity without waste is rewarded, as are her husband and storekeeper; giving from his earnings without permission earns her half his reward.
Whoever wants his provision expanded and his life lengthened should keep good relations with his relatives.
The Prophet bought grain on credit from a Jew, pledging his iron armour, and said Muhammad's household had not a sa of food for the evening meal.
Abu Bakr, serving the Muslims, fed his family from the treasury; companions laboured by hand; the best food is earned by one's own hands, like David's, and woodcutting beats begging.
The Prophet asked Allah's mercy for one lenient in buying, selling and claiming his money; Allah forgave men who gave debtors time and forgave those in hardship.
Buyer and seller truthful about defects are blessed, while liars lose the blessing; bartering two sa of mixed dates for one is forbidden; an Ansari's butcher cooked for the Prophet.
People will not care if gain is lawful; the Prophet banned alcohol trade, dreamt of a riba-eater stoned in a river of blood, and forbade dog prices, tattooing and riba.
Swearing may sell goods but loses Allah's blessing, and a verse on selling Allah's covenant and oaths came down about a man who swore falsely to cheat a Muslim.
Planning to marry Fatima, Ali arranged for a goldsmith of Bani Qainuqa to bring idhkhir with him and sell it to goldsmiths to pay for his wedding banquet.
Allah made Mecca a sanctuary where fighting was allowed the Prophet only a few hours; its shrubs, trees, game and lost things are protected, except idhkhir for goldsmiths and roofs.
Asi bin Wail refused to repay Khabbab the blacksmith unless he disbelieved, mocking that he would pay after resurrection with wealth and children, and a verse came down about him.
The Prophet ate a tailor's meal, picking out the gourd, and wore a sheet a woman wove him, then gave it to a man wanting it for his shroud.
A woman's slave carpenter made the Prophet a pulpit, and when he sat on it the palm stem he used to preach beside cried until he embraced it.
The Prophet bought grain on credit against his armour and bought Jabir's camel, returning it with its price; trade in the Hajj season is allowed; Ibn Umar kept defective camels.
A good companion is like a musk seller whose scent you buy or enjoy, a bad one like a blacksmith's bellows that burns your clothes or leaves a foul smell.
The Prophet paid Abu Taiba a sa of dates for cupping him and had his masters lighten his tax; were the wage unlawful, he would not have paid it.
The Prophet sent Umar a silk garment to benefit from by selling, not to wear, since it is worn by one with no share in the Hereafter.
The Prophet would not enter over a cushion with pictures Aisha bought, saying picture-makers will be told to give them life and angels do not enter houses with pictures.
The Prophet asked Bani Najjar to price their garden; buyer and seller may cancel or confirm until they part, and truthful dealing blesses a deal while lies remove its blessing.
The Prophet bought Umar's camel and gave it straight to Ibn Umar, who left one deal quickly so it stood; a man often cheated was told to say 'no cheating'.
An army attacking the Ka'bah will be swallowed by the earth at Al-Baida', market people and others among them, and all will be resurrected and judged by their intentions.
Prayer in congregation is over twenty times better than at home or market; each step to the mosque raises a degree, and angels pray for one awaiting prayer.
When a man called 'Abul-Qasim' meaning someone else, the Prophet told people to name themselves with his name but not with his kunya.
Going by the Bani Qainuqa market to Fatima's house, the Prophet embraced and kissed his grandson Al-Hasan and asked Allah to love him and whoever loves him.
Food bought from caravans was not to be resold where it was bought but carried to the food market, nor resold before it was received in full measure.
Abdullah bin Amr said the Torah describes the Prophet as witness, bearer of glad tidings and warner, Al-Mutawakkil, neither harsh nor loud in markets, forgiving evildoers, and opening blind eyes.
Food is resold only once its measure is settled; measuring brings blessing; Jabir's measured dates paid his father's debts undiminished, and the Prophet prayed for Medina's mudd and sa.
Food may not be resold before being measured and received, and sellers who had not taken it home were punished; like-for-like exchange is riba unless equal and hand to hand.
When permission to emigrate came, the Prophet told Abu Bakr at noon, accepted his company, and took one of his two prepared she-camels only on paying its price.
The Prophet forbade luring another's buyer, town dwellers selling for desert dwellers, najsh, selling an unborn camel's young, and sales by touching or tossing cloth; he sold a man's slave.
Whoever buys a sheep or camel left unmilked may keep it or return it with a sa of dates; meeting sellers before market, najsh and luring others' buyers are forbidden.
A slave-girl proven to have committed illegal sexual intercourse is lashed by her owner without further blame, and after a third offence sold even for a hair rope.
Aisha was told to buy and free Barirah, the wala' going to the one who frees, and the Prophet declared conditions not in Allah's Book invalid even if a hundred.
Jarir pledged allegiance to the Prophet to testify that none is worshipped but Allah and Muhammad is His Apostle, pray, pay zakat, listen and obey, and advise every Muslim well.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans before they reach market, town dwellers acting as brokers for desert dwellers, and reselling food bought from caravans before carrying it to market.
Barirah's masters insisted on her wala', but the Prophet told Aisha to buy her, as wala' belongs to the one who frees and conditions not in Allah's Book are invalid.
Wheat for wheat, barley for barley and dates for dates are riba unless equal in amount and handed over hand to hand.
The Prophet forbade Muzabana, selling fresh dates or grapes for dried ones by measure, or unmeasured fruit against a measured amount, but allowed selling fruit on trees by estimation.
Gold for gold, silver for silver, must be equal and hand to hand, else riba; gold for silver is allowed, not on credit; Ibn Abbas saw riba only in delay.
Dates may not be sold before safe from blight, nor fresh for dried; Muzabana and Muhaqala are forbidden, but 'Araya owners may sell fruit by estimate, up to five wasqs.
Fruit may not be sold before its benefit is evident, red or yellow, fit to eat, for if Allah spoils it the seller has no right to the buyer's money.
The Prophet bought foodstuff on credit from a Jew and pledged his armour to him.
Learning Khaibar's governor bartered one sa of fine dates for two, the Prophet forbade it as a kind of usury: sell the mixed dates for money, then buy good ones.
Fruits of sold pollinated palms go to the seller unless the buyer stipulates them; Muzabana and similar sales are forbidden, as is selling dates before they turn red or yellow.
Eating fresh dates, the Prophet says one tree resembles a faithful believer; Ibn Umar, the youngest present, kept quiet, and the Prophet names the date palm.
Abu Taiba, a slave, cupped the Prophet, who ordered him paid a Sa of dates and ordered his masters to reduce his tax.
Hind says Abu Sufyan is a miser, and the Prophet lets her and her sons take from his money what is sufficient, reasonably and fairly.
Aisha says verse 4.6 came about the guardian of orphans: a rich guardian takes no wages from their property, a poor one what is just and reasonable for his labour.
The Prophet gave pre-emption in every joint undivided property, but none once the boundaries are marked and the ways and streets fixed.
Three men shut in a cave by a rock each invoke Allah by a deed done for His sake, and the rock moves away bit by bit.
The Prophet asks a pagan driving sheep whether they are for sale or a gift, and buys one sheep from him.
Abraham, emigrating with Sarah, calls her his sister before a tyrant king; her prayers leave the king seized whenever he approaches, and he sends her back with a slave-girl.
A disputed boy goes to Abd bin Zam'a, the child belonging to the bed's owner, though Sauda screens herself; Suhaib, told to claim only his father, says he was kidnapped.
Hakim bin Hizam asks about the kin ties he kept, slaves he freed and alms he gave before Islam, and the Prophet says he embraced Islam with those good deeds.
Passing a dead sheep, the Prophet says its skin could be used, for only eating it is unlawful.
The son of Mary will soon descend as a just ruler, break the Cross, kill the pig and abolish the Jizya; money will then abound and none will accept charity.
Umar curses a seller of alcohol, citing the curse on Jews who sold fat forbidden to them; picture-makers will be punished, and the alcohol trade was made unlawful.
Allah will be against three on Resurrection Day: one who betrays a covenant made in His name, one who sells a free person, and one who withholds a labourer's wages.
Safiya, a captive, was given to Dihya Al-Kalbi, then the Prophet; asked about coitus interruptus with captives, he says it is better not to, as every destined soul will exist.
The Prophet sold a Mudabbar on behalf of his master, who was still living and in need of money.
An unmarried slave-girl proved guilty of illegal sexual intercourse is flogged each time, without further blame, and sold on the third or fourth offence, even for a hair rope.
After Khaibar was conquered the Prophet chose Safiya, whose husband had been killed, married her on the way with a wedding meal of Hais, and helped her mount his camel.

In Mecca's conquest year the Prophet forbids trading alcohol, carcasses, pigs and idols; he forbade a dog's price, money for blood, prostitutes' and soothsayers' earnings, and cursed tattooing and Riba.
Finding Medina's people paying in advance for fruit delivered years later, the Prophet says advance payment must be for a known measure, a known weight and a known period.
Ibn Abi Aufa and Ibn Abza say the companions paid in advance for wheat, barley, raisins and oil of known measure and period, without asking Sham's peasants about crops.
Asked about advance payment for dates, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar say the Prophet forbade selling dates until fit to eat; Ibn Umar adds silver for gold on credit.
The Prophet bought foodstuff from a Jew on credit for a set period and mortgaged his iron armour to him.
Advance payment for fruit is for a fixed measure and period; companions paid Sham peasants in advance without asking about crops; and sale timed by a she-camel's birth is forbidden.
The Prophet ruled pre-emption (Shuf'a) for every undivided joint property, but none once the limits are marked and the ways and streets fixed.
Abu Rafi sells his dwellings to Sa'd below another offer, as the Prophet said a neighbour has more right for his nearness; gifts go first to the nearest door.
An honest treasurer is one of two charitable persons; no post goes to one demanding it; the Prophet shepherded for pay, and he and Abu Bakr hire a pagan guide.
A man who bit another's finger lost his own tooth, and the Prophet, and Abu Bakr in a similar case, rejected his claim for compensation.
Al-Khadir straightens a wall about to fall with his hand, and Moses says he could have taken wages for it to buy food.
Muslims, Jews and Christians are like labourers hired for parts of a day; the Muslims, working from Asr to sunset, get double pay, which Allah calls His blessing.
Allah will oppose three on Resurrection Day: one who betrays a covenant made in His name, one who sells a free person, and one who withholds a labourer's wages.
Labourers who quit at midday and at Asr forfeit their wages, while a last batch working till sunset receives both batches' wages; such are the Muslims, who accepted the guidance.
Three men trapped in a cave by a rock invoke Allah by deeds done for His sake: serving parents, leaving a cousin untouched and paying a labourer's grown wages.
When told to give in charity, the companions worked as porters in the market to earn a Mudd, though some later owned a hundred thousand.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans on the way and a townsman selling for a bedouin, which Ibn Abbas explains as acting as his broker.
Al-As bin Wail will not pay Khabbab unless he disbelieves in Muhammad, promising to pay after resurrection with property and offspring, and a verse is revealed about such a man.
Companions refused hospitality recite Al-Fatiha as Ruqya over a stung chief for a flock of sheep, and the Prophet approves and asks for a share.
The Prophet was cupped and paid the cupper his wages in foodstuff, asking his masters to reduce his tax, and he never withheld anyone's wages.
The Prophet forbade the price of a dog, the earnings of prostitutes and slave-girls by prostitution, a soothsayer's charges, and payment for an animal's copulation.
The Prophet gave Khaibar's land to the Jews to farm for half its yield until Umar evacuated them, while Rafi says the Prophet forbade renting farms.
A rich man delaying repayment is unjust, and a debt transferred to a rich debtor should be accepted; the Prophet prays over a debtor once Abu Qatada takes it on.
Sureties are taken for an adulterer already lashed and for repentant renegades; an Israelite borrower names Allah as witness and surety, and his repayment reaches the lender by sea.
The Prophet's bond of brotherhood let emigrants inherit from Ansar until verse 4.33 ended that; he joined Abdur-Rahman bin Auf with Sa'd and allied Quraish with the Ansar.
The Prophet will not lead a debtor's funeral prayer until Abu Qatada undertakes to pay the debt.
Abu Bakr pays Jabir the Bahrain money the Prophet had promised; in Mecca he returns Ibn Ad-Daghna's protection, content with Allah's, and waits to emigrate with the Prophet.
The Prophet prayed over dead debtors only if they left enough to repay; once wealthy through conquests, he took on believers' debts, their wealth going to their heirs.
Ali distributes the saddles and skins of the slaughtered Budn, and Uqba, left with a kid after sharing out sheep, is told to sacrifice it himself.
Abdur-Rahman bin Auf, under a written pact with Umaiya bin Khalaf, tries to shield him at Badr, but Bilal calls the Ansar, who kill Umaiya and his son.
The Prophet forbids exchanging two Sa of poor dates for one of good Janib dates as Riba: sell the poor dates for money and buy with it.
A slave-girl slaughters a dying sheep with a broken stone, and the Prophet permits eating it.
A creditor, rude in one report, is given an older camel than he was owed, and the Prophet says the best people repay others' rights generously.
The Hawazin delegation, now Muslim, choose their captives over their property, and the Prophet asks the Muslims to return them; their chiefs confirm all gave up their shares willingly.
The Prophet buys Jabir's slow camel, letting him ride it to Medina, approves his marrying a widow to care for his father's daughters, and has Bilal pay extra.
A woman offers herself to the Prophet, and he marries her to a man who asks, for what he knows of the Quran by heart.
Caught thrice stealing the Ramadan Sadaqa, a thief teaches Abu Huraira to recite Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime for protection; the Prophet says he told the truth but was Satan.
Bilal exchanges two Sa of poor dates for one of Barni dates, and the Prophet says it is Riba: sell the poor dates for money, then buy.
The trustee of Umar's Waqf may eat from it and feed friends without amassing wealth; Ibn Umar managed it and gave presents from it.
The Prophet sends Unais to stone a man's wife if she confesses illegal sexual intercourse, and has those present beat a drunk man with shoes and palm-leaf stalks.
Aisha twisted garlands for the Prophet's sacrificial animals, which he sent with her father, and nothing lawful became unlawful for him until they were slaughtered.
Hearing verse 3.92, Abu Talha gives his beloved garden Beeruha in charity and the Prophet suggests he divide it among relatives; an honest treasurer is one of two charitable persons.
Whatever a bird, person or animal eats of what a Muslim plants counts as charity, yet Abu Umama heard the Prophet say humiliation enters any house farming equipment enters.
Keeping a dog not guarding farms or cattle, or hunting, costs a Qirat of reward daily; a cow says it was made for ploughing, and a wolf speaks.
The Prophet declines to divide the Ansar's palms with the emigrants, who instead tend the trees and share the fruit.
The Prophet had the palms of Bani An-Nadir burnt and cut down at Al-Buwaira, as a poem of Hassan bin Thabit recalls.
Renting land for one portion's yield is forbidden; the Prophet let Khaibar's people farm for half its produce, and Ibn Abbas says lending land free is better than renting it.
Three men shut in a cave by a rock invoke Allah by deeds done for His sake, and Allah removes the rock.
Umar would have divided conquered land among the soldiers, as the Prophet did Khaibar, but for later generations; whoever cultivates land belonging to nobody has most right to it.
At Dhul-Hulaifa in the valley of Al-Aqiq the Prophet is told in a dream it is a blessed valley, where he should pray and intend Umrah with Hajj.
Khaibar's Jews farmed for half its fruit until Umar expelled them; Rafi says the Prophet forbade renting farms for produce, Ibn Abbas that lending free is better.
A dweller of Paradise asks Allah to let him farm, and his crop grows mountain-high in a wink; a bedouin says he must be from Quraysh or the Ansar.
The companions were happy on Fridays because an old woman served them cooked silq roots after the Friday prayer, before which they took neither meals nor the midday nap.
Abu Huraira says he narrates much because he stayed with the Prophet while others traded or tended their properties, and after spreading his sheet he forgot nothing of that statement.
The Prophet asks the boy on his right to let elders have his leftover drink, but the boy declines; he also serves a bedouin on his right before Abu Bakr.
The Prophet forbids withholding surplus water, for that keeps people from grazing their cattle.
No blood money is due for death in a mine or well or by an animal, and a fifth of treasure found in one's land is due.
A false oath to take property brings Allah's anger, verse 3.77 confirming it over Al-Ash'ath's well; Allah will not look at one withholding surplus water or swearing falsely over goods.
When an Ansari in an irrigation dispute objects that Az-Zubair is the Prophet's cousin, the Prophet gives Zubair his full right, and Zubair links verse 4.65 to it.
A man who watered a thirsty dog was forgiven, as serving any living being earns reward, and a woman entered Hell for locking up a cat until it starved.
Given a drink, the Prophet asks the boy on his right to let the elders drink first, but the boy declines, so he gives it to him.
The Prophet will drive some people away from his Fount on the Day of Resurrection, as stray camels are driven from a trough.
Had Ishmael's mother left Zamzam as it was, it would be a flowing stream; she let the Jurhum settle by her on condition they had no right to the water.
Allah will not speak to or look at a seller lying on oath about offers, one swearing falsely after Asr to take property, or one withholding surplus water.
No pasture may be reserved as Hima except for Allah and His Apostle; the Prophet made An-Naqi' a Hima, and Umar reserved As-Saraf and Ar-Rabadha for Zakat animals.
Horses bring reward to one keeping them for Allah's cause, shelter to one earning by them, and sin to one keeping them for pride; donkeys fall under the atom's-weight verse.
A finder notes a found thing's container and tie and announces it for a year, then returns it to its owner or uses it; lost sheep are taken, camels left.
Gathering a bundle of firewood and selling it is better than asking people, who may give or refuse.
Hamza, drinking wine, cuts up the she-camels Ali would load with Idhkhir to pay for his wedding banquet, and retorts to the Prophet's rebuke, before drinking was prohibited.
The Ansar decline a land grant in Bahrain unless the emigrants get the same, and the Prophet tells them to be patient with the preference they will see after him.
One of the rights of a she-camel is that it be milked at a place of water.
Fruits of pollinated palms and a sold slave's property go to the seller unless stipulated; Muzabana and similar sales are forbidden, except selling 'Araya dates for ready dates by estimate.
The Prophet pays for Jabir's camel later and mortgages armour for food on credit; Allah repays for a borrower meaning to repay, and he would keep gold only for debts.
The Prophet repays a harsh creditor with an older camel, as the best repay handsomely; a merchant who eased his debtors was forgiven, and Jabir is repaid with extra.
The Prophet blesses Jabir's palms so his father's debts are paid with dates to spare; he seeks refuge from debt and takes on dead believers' debts, heirs getting their property.
Delay by a rich debtor is injustice, a creditor has the right to speak, and one finding his own goods with a bankrupt has most right to them.
A man pledged that his slave would be freed at his death; the Prophet sold the slave to Nu'aim bin Abdullah and gave the price to the owner.
An Israelite lends money for a fixed period; the Prophet measures out Jabir's dates to his dead father's creditors without lessening them, and buys Jabir's tired camel.
A man often cheated in bargaining is told to say 'No deception' whenever he buys, and he did so afterwards.
Allah forbids undutifulness to mothers, burying daughters alive, withholding others' rights and begging, and dislikes idle talk, too many questions and wasting wealth.
Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charge: the ruler for his subjects, a husband for his family, a wife for her husband's house, a servant for his master's property.
A man who recited a verse differently is brought to the Prophet, who says both readings are right and warns that nations before them differed and perished.
After a Muslim slaps a Jew who swore by Moses' superiority, the Prophet forbids preferring him over Moses, whom he will see holding the Throne when all fall unconscious.
A Jew who crushed a girl's head between two stones, named by her nod, confesses, and the Prophet orders his head crushed between two stones.
A man often cheated in buying is told to say 'No cheating' when he buys, and he did so.
A man freed a slave though he had no other property, so the Prophet cancelled it and sold the slave to Nu'aim bin Al-Nahham.
Whoever swears falsely to take a Muslim's property meets an angry Allah; Al-Ash'ath says the verse on oaths sold for little gain came over his land dispute with a Jew.
Hearing Ka'b and Ibn Abi Hadrad argue loudly over a debt in the mosque, the Prophet has Ka'b drop half and tells the debtor to repay the rest.
Umar brings Hisham to the Prophet for reciting Surat al-Furqan differently; the Prophet approves both readings, saying the Quran was revealed in seven ways.
The Prophet says he intended to have the Iqama called and then burn the houses of those who do not attend the prayer.
Abd bin Zam'a and Sa'd dispute a slave-girl's son; the Prophet gives the boy to Abd, as the son goes to the bed's owner, but tells Sauda to screen herself.
Horsemen sent to Najd bring Thumama bin Uthal, chief of Yamama, who is tied to a pillar of the mosque until the Prophet orders his release.
Ka'b, arguing loudly with his debtor, is told by the Prophet's gesture to drop half the debt, and he takes half.
Al-As bin Wail will not repay Khabbab unless he rejects Muhammad, saying he will pay after resurrection with property and offspring, and a verse is revealed about such a man.
Found things are announced for a year, then used but returned if the owner comes; lost sheep are taken, camels left; a lender finds his money in driftwood.
The Prophet would have eaten a date fallen on the road, or on his bed, but for fear it was from Sadaqa.
Mecca's thorny bushes, game and grass are protected, except Idhkhir, and its fallen things may be picked up only to announce them; the speech is written for Abu Shah.
No one should milk another's animal without its owner's permission, for udders are their owners' stores, as no one would want his storeroom broken into.
A found thing is announced for a year, its container and string remembered, and returned if its owner comes; Ubai announced a found purse for up to three years.
Abu Bakr has a Quraishi's shepherd milk a sheep, cools the milk by pouring water over its covered pot, and the Prophet drinks till Abu Bakr is pleased.
Believers settle wrongs among themselves on a bridge before Paradise; Allah screens a believer, has him confess his sins and forgives them, while disbelievers and hypocrites are exposed.
A Muslim is a Muslim's brother, neither oppressing him nor handing him to an oppressor; help your brother, oppressor or oppressed, by stopping his oppression; believers are like a building.
Oppression will be darkness on Resurrection Day, an oppressed person's curse has no screen before Allah, and an oppressor should seek pardon now or repay in good deeds and sins.
Aisha says verse 4.128 concerns a man who dislikes his wife and means to divorce her, and she gives up her rights so that he keeps her.
Given a drink, the Prophet asks the boy on his right to let the old men have the rest, but the boy declines, so he hands him the bowl.
Whoever unjustly takes even a span of another's land will have it encircling his neck down the seven earths, or will sink down them, on the Day of Resurrection.
The Prophet forbade eating two dates at a time without one's companions' permission, and asks Abu Shu'aib's permission for an uninvited man who followed him to the meal.
The most quarrelsome is most hated by Allah; the Prophet, being human, may mistakenly rule for the more eloquent party, and what is wrongly given is a portion of Fire.
Whoever lies when he speaks, breaks his promises, betrays covenants and is insulting in quarrels is a hypocrite, and one of these traits is a trait of hypocrisy.
Hind may feed her children from the property of Abu Sufyan, whom she calls a miser, if she does so justly and reasonably.
Companions the Prophet sends out may accept due hospitality from their hosts, and take a guest's right from those who refuse it.
When the Prophet died, the Ansar assembled in the shed of Bani Sa'ida, and Umar and Abu Bakr went to them.
No one should stop his neighbour fixing a wooden peg in his wall, Abu Huraira narrates despite his hearers' reluctance.
When alcohol is prohibited, Anas spills Abu Talha's wine into Medina's streets, and a verse says believers who did good are not blamed for what they consumed before.
Those who must sit on the roads are to give the road its rights: lowering the gaze, not harming people, returning greetings, and enjoining good and forbidding evil.
A man who climbed down a well to water a thirsty dog was forgiven, as serving any living being earns reward.
From a high building in Medina the Prophet says he sees afflictions falling among their houses as thickly as raindrops.
Umar names Aisha and Hafsa as the two wives in verse 66:4 and tells how the Prophet kept away from his wives twenty-nine days, then offered them a choice.
Jabir brings the camel to the mosque, telling the Prophet it is his, and the Prophet, after examining it, says both the camel and its price are Jabir's.
The Prophet came to some people's rubbish dump and urinated there standing.
Allah thanked and forgave a man who removed a thorny branch from the road.
In a dispute about land the Prophet ruled that seven cubits be left as a public way.
The Prophet forbade robbery and mutilation, and said an adulterer, a drinker of alcohol, a thief or a robber is not a believer while committing the act.
The Hour will not come before the son of Mary descends as a just ruler, breaks the cross, kills the pigs and abolishes the jizya, and money abounds unaccepted.
At Khaibar the Prophet ordered the pots cooking donkey meat to be emptied and broken, then allowed them to be washed instead.
Entering Mecca, the Prophet struck the three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'bah with a stick, reciting that truth has come and falsehood has vanished.
The Prophet tore Aisha's curtain decorated with pictures, and she made it into two cushions that he sat on.
Whoever is killed while protecting his property is a martyr.
When one wife broke a bowl of food sent by another, the Prophet gathered the food, kept the broken bowl and sent back an unbroken one.
Juraij, an Israelite, ignored his mother's call while praying; she prayed he would see prostitutes' faces, a woman claimed her baby was his, and the baby named the shepherd.
Short of food, Abu Ubaida's army and the Ash'aris pooled their provisions and shared them equally, the Prophet blessed a pooled heap, and a camel's meat was split ten ways.
Abu Bakr's written law of zakat says partners in jointly owned sheep pay its zakat equally.
The Prophet overturned pots of hastily cooked booty, counted ten sheep as a camel, and allowed shooting a runaway camel and slaughter with what spills blood, not teeth or nails.
The Prophet forbade eating two dates at a time without the permission of one's companions at the meal.
Whoever frees his share of a jointly owned slave must free him fully if he can afford the rest; otherwise he is partly freed or works, unburdened, to earn it.
Those who keep Allah's limits and those who break them are like people in a boat: if the upper deck stops the lower from holing it, all are saved.
Aisha explains verse 4:3: guardians tempted by an orphan girl's wealth and beauty must give her a fair mahr and treat her justly, or else marry other women.
The right of pre-emption holds in every jointly owned property until the land is divided and its ways are marked out.
Partners who bought partly in cash and partly on credit were told by the Prophet to keep what was hand to hand and leave what was on credit.
The Prophet rented the land of Khaibar to the Jews on condition that they work and cultivate it for half of its yield.
Given sheep to distribute among the companions for sacrifice, Uqba was told to sacrifice the leftover kid himself.
The Prophet blessed the young Abdullah bin Hisham instead of taking his pledge, and later Ibn Umar and Ibn Az-Zubair sought him as their partner in buying foodstuff.
Whoever frees his share of a jointly owned slave must free him fully, paying his partners, if he can afford it; otherwise the slave works for it without overburdening.
In Ihram for Hajj at Mecca, companions were told to make it Umrah and leave Ihram; the Prophet, with his sacrificial animal, stayed in Ihram and shared it with Ali.
At Dhul-Hulaifa the Prophet overturned pots of hastily cooked booty, counted a camel as ten sheep, and allowed slaughter with what spills blood, but not teeth or nails.
The Prophet mortgaged his armour for barley bought on credit, and said Muhammad's household of nine houses had only a sa' of grain for morning and evening.
When the Prophet asked who would kill Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf for harming Allah and His Messenger, Muhammad bin Maslama sought a loan, offering arms in pledge, then killed him.
A mortgaged animal may be ridden and a mortgaged milch animal milked by the one who feeds it, and the Prophet mortgaged his armour to a Jew for foodstuff.
The Prophet ruled that the defendant takes an oath when the claimant has no two witnesses, and whoever swears falsely to seize property meets Allah angry, as verse 3:77 confirms.
Freeing a Muslim slave saves the freer's body from the Fire, the best manumission is of the costliest and most loved slave, and the Prophet ordered slaves freed at eclipses.
Whoever frees his share of a jointly owned slave must free him wholly, paying co-owners a just price, if able; otherwise the slave is partly freed or works for it.
Allah forgives the heart's whispers that are not acted on or spoken, and deeds are rewarded by intention, so a migration counts for what one migrated for.
Abu Huraira's slave, lost on the way to Islam, reappeared while he was with the Prophet, and Abu Huraira freed him for Allah's sake.
The Prophet gave the son of Zam'a's slave-girl to Abd bin Zam'a, born on his father's bed, though Sa'd claimed him for Utba, and told Sauda to veil from him.
The Prophet sold a slave promised freedom at his master's death, forbade selling or giving away wala', and had Aisha free Barirah, who chose freedom over her husband.
The Prophet refused the Ansar's request to give up even a dirham of the ransom of their nephew Al-Abbas.
Hakim bin Hizam freed slaves and slaughtered camels before and after Islam, and the Prophet told him he had embraced Islam with all the good deeds he had done.
Muslims willingly returned Hawazin's captives, Bani Mustaliq's women and children were taken in a surprise attack, and coitus interruptus with captives was discouraged, as destined souls will come.
Abu Huraira loves Bani Tamim for three sayings: they will stand firm against the Dajjal, their charity is 'our folk's', and their slave-girl should be freed as Ishmael's descendant.
A man who educates, frees and marries his slave-girl, and a slave serving his master and worshipping Allah well, get double reward; slaves are brethren, fed and clothed alike.
Say 'my master' rather than 'your lord' of an owner, and 'my lad' or 'my lass' rather than 'my slave' or 'my slave-girl'.
Whoever frees his share of a common slave must pay the rest of his just price and free him if he can afford it; otherwise the slave is partly freed.
Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charge: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's house, a slave for his master's property.
A slave-girl who commits illegal sexual intercourse is scourged each time, and after the third or fourth offence is sold even for a hair rope.
A servant who brings his master's meal should be seated to share it, or at least be given a mouthful or two, since he prepared it.
Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charge, from the ruler, the man and the woman to the servant over his master's property and a man over his father's property.
Whoever fights or beats someone should avoid the face.
Barirah sought Aisha's help with her emancipation contract; her masters demanded her wala', but the Prophet said wala' is for the liberator and conditions not in Allah's laws are invalid.
No woman should belittle a neighbour's gift, even a sheep's trotter; the Prophet accepted such gifts, and his household, cooking nothing for months, lived on dates, water and neighbours' milk.
At the Prophet's request a woman had her carpenter slave make him a pulpit of tamarisk wood, which he placed where it now stands.
Abu Qatada, not in Ihram, killed an onager that his companions in Ihram would not help him hunt, and the Prophet, in Ihram, ate the foreleg he had kept.
Given milk mixed with water, the Prophet passed the rest to the bedouin on his right rather than to Abu Bakr, saying to begin from the right.
The Prophet accepted and ate the thighs of a rabbit Anas caught, but declined an onager presented while he was in Ihram, explaining this to the saddened giver.
People sent gifts on Aisha's day; the Prophet ate gifts but not charity, saying charity given to Barirah was a gift for him, and left a gifted mastigar he disliked.
Um Salama's group of wives asked that gifts reach the Prophet in any wife's house; he said revelation came to him only in Aisha's bed, and Aisha silenced Zainab.
Anas, like the Prophet, would not refuse gifts of perfume.
The Prophet asked the Muslims to return the repentant Hawazin's captives as a favour or for later compensation, and they agreed willingly.
The Prophet accepted gifts and gave in return, and told a father who had given one son a slave to be just to his children and take the gift back.
In his serious illness the Prophet, with his wives' leave, was nursed in Aisha's house, walking there supported between Al-Abbas and Ali with his feet dragging.
One who takes back his gift is like a dog that swallows its vomit.
Asma, whose only property came from Az-Zubair, was told to give in charity and not withhold or give reluctantly, lest Allah withhold from her.
Maimuna was told giving her slave-girl to her maternal uncles would have earned more than freeing her; the Prophet drew lots among his wives, and Sauda gave Aisha her turn.
Asked which of two neighbours should get her gift, Aisha was told the one whose door is nearer.
The Prophet declined As-Sa'b's gift of onager meat at Al-Abwa' or Waddan because he was in Ihram, and told the saddened giver so.
A zakat collector who claimed presents given to him was asked whether he would have got them at home; whoever takes zakat unlawfully will carry it on his neck.
Abu Bakr paid Jabir what the Prophet had promised him from Bahrain's funds, and the Prophet kept a cloak aside for Makhrama from those he distributed.
A man who had intercourse while fasting in Ramadan could not free a slave, fast two months or feed sixty poor, so dates given for expiation went to his family.
When creditors harshly demanded the debt of Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, the Prophet blessed his date-palms, and their fruit paid them in full with much left over.
Offered a drink, the Prophet asked the boy on his right to let the old men on his left drink first, but the boy would not yield his share.
The Prophet paid Jabir what he owed him and more, weighing out the price of the camel Jabir had sold him with an extra amount.
The boy on the Prophet's right refused to give up his turn to the old men on his left, so the Prophet put the bowl in his hand.
When a creditor demanded his debt harshly, the Prophet stopped his companions, saying he had the right to speak, and repaid him an older camel, as the best repay best.
Hawazin's delegation, made to choose between their property and their captives, chose the captives, and the Muslims, through their leaders, agreed willingly to return them.
Owing a camel of a certain age, the Prophet let its owner demand it and repaid him an older camel, saying the best repay their debts most handsomely.
The Prophet bought Umar's troublesome camel, which kept going ahead of him, and gave it to Abdullah bin Umar to do with as he liked.
Calling a silk cloak the dress of one with no share in the Hereafter, the Prophet sent Umar one not to wear, and Umar gave it to a pagan brother.
The Prophet would not enter Fatima's house because of a decorated curtain, saying he had no interest in worldly things, and had it sent to needy people.
Ali cut up a silk dress the Prophet gave him on seeing his anger, and of a silk cloak from Ukaidir the Prophet said Sa'd's handkerchiefs in Paradise are better.
A Jewess brought the Prophet a poisoned sheep and he ate of it; he refused to have her killed, and Anas kept seeing the poison's effect in his mouth.
With 130 companions, the Prophet bought a sheep from a pagan, gave everyone a piece of its roasted organs, and its meat filled two basins, with food left over.
The Prophet sent Umar a silk cloak not to wear but to sell or give away, and Umar sent it to his brother in Mecca, not yet a Muslim.
Asma asked whether to keep good relations with her pagan mother who had come to her, and the Prophet said yes.
Taking back a gift is like a dog swallowing its vomit, so Umar was told not to buy back, even for a dirham, a horse he gave in Allah's cause.
Asma was told to keep good relations with her polytheist mother, who came to her in the Prophet's lifetime.
The Prophet ruled that an umra belongs to the one to whom it is presented, and that it is permissible.
When Medina was alarmed, the Prophet borrowed Abu Talha's horse Al-Mandub, rode out, found nothing to fear, and praised the horse's speed.
Aisha, in a coarse five-dirham dress, says that in the Prophet's time women wishing to look elegant would borrow such a dress from her.
Lending a milch animal is a fine charity, best of forty deeds; land is better given free than rented, and the Ansar's gifted palms were returned after Khaibar.
Abraham migrated with Sarah, who was given Hajar as a slave-girl, and Sarah said Allah had humiliated the pagan.
Umar was told not to buy back a horse he had given in Allah's cause, as one should not take back what one gave in charity.
When liars accused Aisha, the Prophet consulted Ali and Usama, Barirah found no fault in her but youth, and he asked for help against the man who defamed his family.
The Prophet hid behind date-palms to overhear Ibn Saiyad, but his mother alerted him, and the Prophet said he would otherwise have revealed his reality.
A woman finally divorced by Rifa'a and remarried was told she cannot return to him without full relations with her present husband.
When a woman said she had suckled Uqba and his wife, the Prophet asked how he could keep her, so he divorced her.
Umar says that since revelation has ended people are judged by their public deeds, their secrets left to Allah.
Paradise or Hell is affirmed for the dead whom people praise or blame, for believers are Allah's witnesses on earth, and even two attesting a Muslim's good character suffice.
Foster relations count like blood relations: Aisha's foster uncle may visit her, Hamza's daughter is unlawful to the Prophet, and fostership is valid only in the suckling period.
A woman's hand was cut off for theft at the Conquest, after which she repented and married, and an unmarried adulterer was ordered a hundred lashes and a year's exile.
The Prophet refused to witness an unequal gift to one son as injustice, and foretold people after the best generations who give witness unasked and break their vows.
The great sins are associating others with Allah, undutifulness to parents, murder and false witness, against which the Prophet warned repeatedly.
Hearing a man recite in the mosque, the Prophet asked mercy for him for recalling verses he had dropped, and asked mercy for Abbad on recognising his voice.
Bilal's adhan comes while it is still night, so eat and drink until the blind Ibn Um Maktum's adhan at dawn.
Knowing Makhrama's voice at the door, the Prophet came out with a garment he had kept for him, praising its qualities.
Asked whether a woman's witness is not half a man's, the women agreed, and the Prophet said this is because of the deficiency of a woman's mind.
When a black slave-woman said she had suckled Uqba and his wife, the Prophet told him to leave her.
Aisha tells how, left behind seeking her necklace, she was falsely accused, fell ill for a month, and was declared innocent by revelation, after which Abu Bakr resumed helping Mistah.
The Prophet said exaggerated praise cuts a man's neck or back; one should only say 'I think him so', vouching for no one before Allah.
Ibn Umar, refused for Uhud at fourteen, was allowed into the Trench battle at fifteen, the age a caliph called the limit of manhood; Friday bathing binds those reaching puberty.
In a dispute without evidence the defendant swears, and whoever swears falsely to seize a Muslim's property meets Allah angry, as verse 3:77, revealed about Al-Ash'ath, confirms.
When Hilal bin Umaiya accused his wife of adultery, the Prophet told him to bring proof or be lashed, then mentioned the li'an as in the Book.
Allah will not speak to one withholding surplus water, pledging to a ruler for gain or lying on oath in a sale, and false oaths for property anger Him.
A man asking about Islam is told of the five daily prayers, Ramadan's fast and zakat, more being voluntary, and will succeed if true to his word.
Whoever has to take an oath should swear by Allah or remain silent.
The Prophet may rule for the more persuasive party, but whatever is wrongly given that way is a piece of fire not to be taken.
Heraclius called keeping promises and trusts a prophet's quality, a hypocrite breaks promises, Abu Bakr paid what the Prophet promised Jabir, and Moses completed the longer term.
Ibn Abbas asks why Muslims question the people of the Scriptures, who changed their books, when they recite the Quran, Allah's latest and undistorted revelation.
Those keeping Allah's limits and those violating them are like people in a boat: stopping one who holes its bottom saves everyone, while leaving him destroys all.
When Um Al-Ala testified that Allah had blessed the dead Uthman bin Mazun, the Prophet said even he did not know what would be done to him.
The Prophet drew lots among his wives for journeys and gave each a day and night, and Sauda gave hers to Aisha.
If people knew the reward of the call to prayer and the first row they would cast lots for them, and they would crawl to the Fajr and Isha prayers.
While the Prophet made peace among Bani Amr bin Auf, Abu Bakr led the prayer and stepped back when he came; men should say Subhan Allah, clapping being for women.
The Prophet went to reconcile quarrelling people, a verse orders peace between fighting believers, a peacemaker saying good things is no liar, and spouses may reconcile on terms.
A bedouin ransomed his son, who committed adultery with his employer's wife, but the Prophet returned the ransom, ordered a hundred lashes and a year's exile, and had her stoned.
Whatever is innovated that is not in harmony with the principles of the religion is rejected.
At Hudaibiya the Prophet rubbed out 'Allah's Messenger' from the treaty, agreed to return pagans who came to him, and came the next year for three days with sheathed weapons.
Abdullah bin Sahl and Muhaiyisa went to Khaibar while it had a peace treaty with the Muslims.
When Ar-Rabi' broke a girl's tooth the Prophet ordered retaliation as Allah's law, but the girl's family forgave and accepted compensation, as Anas bin An-Nadr had sworn.
Al-Hasan bin Ali made peace with Muawiya on guaranteed terms, as the Prophet had said Allah may make peace between two great Muslim groups through this son of his.
The Prophet settled loud debt disputes: one who swore not to ease his debtor gave way, and Ka'b remitted half of what Ibn Abu Hadrad owed him.
Charity is due for every joint of the body, and each day establishing justice among people earns the reward of charity.
When an Ansari objected that Az-Zubair was the Prophet's cousin in their irrigation dispute, the Prophet gave Zubair his full right, and Zubair links a verse on accepting his judgement.
The Prophet blessed the dates of Jabir's indebted father so all creditors were paid with thirteen wasqs left, and had Ka'b remit half of Ibn Abu Hadrad's debt.
At Hudaibiya Suhail made the Prophet agree to return anyone coming from them, so Abu Jandal was returned, but believing women emigrants were not, as a verse was revealed.
The Prophet took believing women's pledge of allegiance by words alone, never touching a woman's hand, and men pledged to pray, pay zakat and give good advice to every Muslim.
Fruit of sold pollinated date-palms belongs to the seller unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.
Barirah's masters would let Aisha buy and free her only if her wala' stayed theirs, and the Prophet told Aisha to buy and free her.
Jabir sells his camel stipulating the ride home; Ansar gardens and Khaibar are worked for shares of fruit; marriage conditions bind most; renting land for a plot's yield is banned.
No town-dweller may sell for a bedouin, nor anyone practise najsh, outbid a brother, propose over his engagement, or a woman seek her sister's divorce to take her place.
A son's ransom of sheep and a slave girl for adultery with his employer's wife is returned; the Prophet orders him lashed and exiled, and the wife stoned on confessing.
Aisha is told to buy and free Barirah though her masters stipulate her wala', for the wala' belongs to the liberator even against a hundred conditions.
The Prophet forbade intercepting caravans, a resident buying for a bedouin, a woman stipulating a rival wife's divorce, spoiling another's bargain, najsh, and holding milk in udders to deceive.
Moses broke his agreement with al-Khadir first by forgetting, then agreed al-Khadir could leave him if he asked again, and on the third occasion asked deliberately, invoking that condition.
Conditions outside Allah's laws are void, so Barirah's wala' goes to her freer; Umar exiles Khaibar's Jews, whose contract let them stay while Allah allowed, paying for their property.
The Prophet accepts Suhail's terms at al-Hudaibiya, including returning converts; companions sacrifice and shave, emigrant women are examined, and Quraish ask him to call in Abu Basir's raiders.
The Prophet mentioned a man who asked an Israelite to lend him a thousand dinars, and was lent them for a fixed period.
Aisha is told to buy and free Barirah, and from the pulpit the Prophet declares conditions not in Allah's laws invalid even if a hundred are stipulated.
Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one, and whoever knows them will go to Paradise.
Advised by the Prophet, Umar makes his best Khaibar land an endowment never sold, gifted or inherited, its yield for the poor, kin, freeing slaves, Allah's cause, travellers and guests.
Wills are to be written within two nights; the Prophet left little and bequeathed Allah's Book; Aisha denies a will for Ali; Sa'd's bequest is limited to a third.
Sa'd claims Zam'a's slave girl's son for his brother Utba; the Prophet gives him to Abd bin Zam'a, the child belonging to the bed, telling Sauda to screen herself.
A Jew who crushed a girl's head between two stones, named by her nod and then confessing, had his head crushed with stones on the Prophet's order.
Once offspring inherited and parents only by will, until Allah set shares: a male double a female, a sixth for each parent, and fixed shares for wife and husband.
The best charity is given while healthy, greedy and fearing poverty, not delayed to the deathbed, when the property already belongs to the heirs.
The signs of a hypocrite are three: he lies when he speaks, betrays when entrusted, and breaks his promises.
The Prophet tells Hakim bin Hizam that wealth taken without greed is blessed and the giving hand better, so Hakim never asks again, refusing even his booty share.
Everyone is a guardian responsible for his charge: the ruler for his subjects, a man for his family, a lady for her husband's house, a servant for his master's property.
When 'Warn your nearest kinsmen' came, the Prophet called Quraysh's clans, Safiya and Fatima, saying he cannot save them from Allah's punishment; Abu Talha divides a garden among relatives.
Seeing a man driving his sacrificial camel, the Prophet told him repeatedly to ride it, adding 'woe to you' when he protested it was for sacrifice.
Sa'd gives a garden and must fulfil a vow for his dead mother; Ka'b keeps some property, Abu Talha's garden goes to relatives, and heirs give at the division.
Aisha explains verses 4.2-3: a guardian drawn to an orphan girl's beauty and wealth may marry her only with a full dowry like her peers', otherwise he marries other women.
Umar makes his prized palm garden Thamgh an endowment never sold, gifted or bequeathed, its fruits for charity, its administrator eating fairly without growing rich.
Aisha says verse 4.6 came about an orphan's guardian: if he is poor, he may take what is just and reasonable from the orphan's wealth.
Avoid seven destructive sins: associating others with Allah, sorcery, unjust killing, consuming usury, consuming an orphan's wealth, fleeing the battlefield, and accusing chaste believing women.
Ibn Umar never refused guardianship, Ibn Sirin liked guardians to meet on an orphan's good, Tawus cited verse 2.220, and Ata said guardians provide for orphans from their shares.
Abu Talha brought the boy Anas to serve the Prophet at home and on journeys, and the Prophet never asked him why he did or left anything.
Abu Talha gives his beloved garden Bairuha for Allah's sake and, on the Prophet's advice, divides it among relatives; a man gives a garden in charity for his dead mother.
Banu an-Najjar will take their garden's price for the mosque only from Allah, and Umar, advised by the Prophet, makes his Khaibar land an endowment never sold, gifted or bequeathed.
Umar asks whether he may buy back the horse he gave in charity for fighting, and is told not to, for one should not take back charity.
The Prophet's heirs will not inherit a dinar or dirham, for what he leaves beyond his wives' support and his employees' wages is charity.
Umar's endowment lets its administrator eat and feed a friend without storing; besieged, Uthman recalls buying the well of Ruma and equipping Tabuk's army; Banu an-Najjar seek only Allah's price.
Two men swear a dead companion's silver bowl was lost; when it turns up, his relatives swear their testimony truer, and the verse 'When death approached any of you' came.
Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, left heavy debts; the Prophet sat on the biggest date heap and measured out until all were paid, the heaps still seeming whole.
Jihad follows timely prayer and kindness to parents, no deed equals it, women's best jihad is Hajj, and the Prophet dreams of followers fighting at sea, Umm Haram among them.
Paradise has a hundred grades for fighters and a house of martyrs; a morning or evening in Allah's cause outweighs the world, and martyrs wish to be killed again.
But for men he cannot mount, the Prophet would join every army unit, and he wishes repeated martyrdom; he announces Zaid, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha martyred, and Khalid victorious.
The Prophet dreamt of followers sailing the sea like kings on thrones, Umm Haram among the first; she joined Mu'awiya's naval expedition and died falling from her mount on return.
Of seventy sent to Bani Amir, all but a lame man are killed after the envoy's stabbing; Gabriel says their Lord is pleased; the Prophet curses the killers forty days.
The Prophet tells his bleeding finger its wound is in Allah's cause; anyone wounded in His cause comes on Resurrection Day with a wound coloured like blood, scented like musk.
Heraclius tells Abu Sufyan that apostles are tested by battles of alternating success, but the final victory is always theirs.
Anas bin an-Nadr falls at Uhud with over eighty wounds, the verse on such men found with Khuzaima; a convert soon martyred is richly rewarded, and Haritha is in Firdaus.
Whoever fights so that Allah's word is highest fights in His cause, and one whose feet are covered with dust in His cause will not be touched by the Fire.
While building the mosque the Prophet wipes dust from Ammar, who carries two bricks at a time, saying a rebellious group will kill him as he calls them to Allah.
Returning from the Trench, the Prophet has bathed when Gabriel, dust on his head, says he has not put down arms and points him toward Bani Quraiza.
The Prophet curses Bir Mauna's killers thirty days; some who drank alcohol that morning are martyred at Uhud; angels shade Jabir's slain father; Paradise is under the shades of swords.
Solomon swore a hundred women would each bear a knight for Allah's cause but did not say 'Allah willing', so only one bore a half-man; had he, all would have.
The Prophet, best, bravest and most generous, rides out ahead when Medina takes fright, and, mobbed by bedouins after Hunain, says they will find him no miser, liar or coward.
Sa'd teaches his sons the Prophet's refuge after prayer from cowardice, decrepit old age, worldly trials and the grave's punishment; the Prophet also sought refuge from helplessness and laziness.
As-Sa'ib heard none of Talha, Sa'd, al-Miqdad and Abdur-Rahman bin Auf narrate from the Prophet, except Talha, who talked about the day of Uhud.
On the day of the Conquest the Prophet says there is no emigration after it, only jihad and intention, and those called to fight must go forth at once.
Allah smiles at a martyr and his killer, later forgiven and martyred, both entering Paradise; at Khaibar a son of Sa'id says Allah honoured through him a Muslim he killed.
Abu Talha did not fast in the Prophet's lifetime because of jihad, but after his death was never seen without fasting except on the two Eids.
Five are martyrs: those who die of plague, abdominal disease, drowning, or a falling building, and those killed in Allah's cause; plague is martyrdom for every Muslim.
When the verse ranking those who strive above those who sit at home came, the blind Ibn Umm Maktum complained, and revelation added the exception for the disabled.
Abdullah bin Abi Aufa wrote that the Prophet said to be patient when facing the enemy.
Digging the trench, cold and hungry Emigrants and Ansar pledge lifelong jihad, while the Prophet, carrying earth, asks Allah to forgive and bless them and grant calm and firm feet.
Anas recalls returning from Tabuk, and on a campaign the Prophet said those held back in Medina by an excuse share the reward of every pass and valley crossed.
Fasting one day for Allah's pleasure keeps one's face seventy years from the Fire, and whoever spends two things in His cause is called by all Paradise's gatekeepers.

The Prophet fears only worldly blessings: wealth is sweet vegetation, excellent when lawfully gained and spent on Allah's cause, orphans, the poor and travellers; the unlawful taker is never satisfied.
Equipping a fighter or caring well for his family earns a fighter's reward, and the Prophet visits Umm Sulaim out of pity, her brother having been killed with him.
At Yamama Thabit bin Qais, perfuming himself with hunut, takes his place and refuses to flee; on the day of the Clans az-Zubair volunteers to scout, called the Prophet's disciple.
Leaving the Prophet, Malik bin al-Huwairith and a friend are told to give the adhan and iqama themselves and let the elder lead the prayer.
Good remains in horses' foreheads till Resurrection, bringing reward or booty; a horse kept for Allah's cause earns reward for its feed and dung; horses named al-Jarada and al-Luhaif appear.
Mu'adh, riding behind the Prophet on the donkey Ufair, learns that Allah's right is to be worshipped alone, and that He will not punish those who worship none besides Him.
When Medina took fright, the Prophet borrowed a horse called Mandub, rode out, found nothing to fear, and said the horse was very fast.
The Prophet said evil omen is in three things, the horse, the woman and the house, or, in another wording, if it is in anything it is in these.
Horses bring reward, shelter or sin; the Prophet speeds Jabir's tired camel and buys it, finds Mandub fast, and gives a horse two booty shares, its rider one.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain when Hawazin's archers turned on Muslims collecting booty, but stayed on his white mule declaring himself the Prophet in truth.
As his foot entered the stirrup and his she-camel rose with him, the Prophet began the Talbiya at the mosque of Dhul-Hulaifa.
The Prophet rode an unsaddled horse, sword slung on, Abu Talha's slow horse became unbeatable, he arranged horse races over set courses, and his she-camel al-Adba was once outrun.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain; the hasty fled when Hawazin shot at them, while he rode his white mule declaring he was the Prophet in truth.
Women's jihad is Hajj; Umm Haram asks to join the sea fighters; the Prophet draws lots among his wives; women carry water, treat the wounded, bring back the dead.
Abu Amir has an arrow drawn from his knee and the Prophet asks forgiveness for him; Sa'd comes armed at night to guard the Prophet, who then sleeps.
May the slave of dinar, dirham and fine clothes, pleased only when given, perish, while Paradise is for the dusty fighter holding his horse's reins, content at front or rear.
An older companion serves Anas, having vowed to serve any Ansari; Anas serves the Prophet; those not fasting serve and take the reward; helping a rider is charity.
Guarding Muslims from unbelievers for one day in Allah's cause, a whip's space in Paradise, and a morning or evening journey in His cause are each better than the world.
Serving the Prophet on the Khaibar expedition, Anas hears his prayers for refuge, sees him marry Safiya with a feast of hais, and hears him make Medina a sanctuary.
Waking from a nap, the Prophet tells Umm Haram of followers voyaging like kings on thrones, she among the first; returning from jihad, she falls and breaks her neck.
Sa'd is told victory and provision come only through the poor among them; armies are given victory while one among them has accompanied the Prophet, then his companions, then theirs.
A fierce fighter the Prophet places among the people of the Fire kills himself when wounded; one may seem to do Paradise's deeds yet belong to the Fire.
The Prophet urges Bani Aslam to practise archery, as their father Ishmael was an archer, and at Badr orders arrows shot when the enemy comes near.
When Umar hits Ethiopians playing before the Prophet with a stone, the Prophet tells him to let them play; a sub-narrator adds that this was in the mosque.
The Prophet shares Abu Talha's shield, and Fatima stops his bleeding when his helmet is smashed; Bani an-Nadir's fai buys arms and horses; Sa'd is urged to shoot.
On Eid the Prophet tells Abu Bakr to leave two girls singing songs of Bu'ath, and lets Aisha watch from behind him as Bani Arfida play with shields and spears.
The Prophet rides with a sword at his neck; conquerors' swords bore no gold or silver; a bedouin who seized his sword is spared; Abu Qatada spears an onager.
In his tent at Badr, in armour, the Prophet pleads for Allah's promise until Abu Bakr says it is enough, then goes out reciting that the multitude will be routed.
The Prophet died while his iron armour was mortgaged to a Jew for thirty sa' of barley.
The miser and the charitable are like two men in tight iron cloaks: giving spreads the giver's cloak over him, while the miser's rings tighten and will not widen.
After relieving himself, the Prophet made ablution in a tight-sleeved Sha'mi cloak, drawing his arms out from beneath it, and wiped over his head and leather socks.
The Prophet allowed Abdur-Rahman bin Auf and az-Zubair to wear silk because of itching from a skin disease or lice, and they wore it in battle.
