The Prophet ate from a sheep's shoulder, cutting it with a knife, then put the knife down when called and prayed without repeating his ablution.
Paradise awaits the Prophet's first followers to sail on expedition, Umm Haram among them; the first army to invade Caesar's City is forgiven, but she is not in it.
Before the Hour Muslims will fight the Jews until a stone tells of a Jew hiding behind it, and fight the Turks, small-eyed and flat-nosed, and people in hair shoes.
The Prophet seeks victory at Hunain, invokes fire and defeat on the Clans, prays for weak Muslims, against Mudar and named men of Quraish, and answers Jews' death-wish in kind.
The Prophet writes to Caesar that rejecting Islam brings his people's sins on him, prays for Daus's guidance, seals letters with a silver ring, and Khusrau tears up his letter.
The Prophet's letter invites Caesar to Islam; Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan, finds in his answers the qualities of a prophet, and his court breaks into uproar.
At Khaibar the Prophet cures Ali's eyes, gives him the flag and tells him to invite them to Islam first, one convert through him being better than red camels.
The Prophet attacked only after dawn, holding back if he heard the adhan; reaching Khaibar by night, he attacked at daybreak, saying Khaibar is ruined.
The Prophet was ordered to fight people until they say none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, which saves their life and property, their account resting with Allah.
Before campaigns the Prophet hid his real destination, except for Tabuk, a long march in great heat against a large enemy, when he told the Muslims so they could prepare.
The Prophet usually set out on Thursdays, Tabuk included; he set out after Zuhr at Medina, five days before Dhul Qa'da ended for Hajj, and in Ramadan, fasting until Kadid.
Sending an expedition, the Prophet first orders two named men of Quraish burnt, then withdraws it at the farewell: only Allah punishes with fire, so kill them if captured.
Obey the ruler except in disobedience to Allah; obeying the Prophet is obeying Allah, obeying the chief is obeying him, and the Imam is a shield to fight behind.
Companions recall pledging allegiance to the Prophet under the tree, for patience or death, the Ansar for jihad at the Trench, and, migration being over, for Islam and jihad.
Asked whether to obey a commander ordering what they cannot do, Abdullah says he does not know, but one stays well while obeying Allah and should ask about doubtful things.
The Prophet told the people not to wish to meet the enemy but be patient when they do, for Paradise is under swords' shade, and asked Allah to defeat them.
On a campaign the Prophet's prayer speeds Jabir's tired camel; he buys it, letting Jabir ride it home, hears why he wed a matron, then pays and returns it.
When Medina was alarmed the Prophet rode Abu Talha's horse out alone, found nothing to fear, and said the horse, once slow, was very fast.
Umar gave a horse for Allah's Cause and later saw it being sold; the Prophet told him not to buy it, as that would take back his charity.
The Prophet would join every army unit but lacks mounts for his followers and dislikes them staying behind; he wishes to be martyred in Allah's Cause, revived and martyred again.
At Tabuk, Yali gives a camel for jihad; his hired worker's quarrel ends with a bitten hand pulled free and a tooth lost, and the Prophet rejects the biter's claim.
Flag-bearer Qais bin Sa'd combs his hair for Hajj; at Khaibar the flag goes to Ali, who came despite eye trouble; Az-Zubair is told where to fix the flag.
The Prophet was given concise speech, victory through awe and the keys of the world's treasures; after Heraclius reads his letter, Abu Sufyan sees the Byzantine king fearing him.
Asma ties the Prophet's emigration food with her belt; sacrificial meat and Sawiq serve as journey food, the Prophet blesses dwindling provisions, and a huge fish feeds 300 men.
Aisha, regretting she returns with Hajj only, is sent behind her brother Abdur-Rahman on his mount to perform Umrah from at-Tan'im while the Prophet waits.
Companions ride double: Anas behind Abu Talha, and Usama behind the Prophet on a donkey and on his camel at the Conquest, when he entered and prayed in the Ka'bah.
Each joint owes daily charity: judging justly, helping a rider mount or load up, a good word, steps to prayer and removing harm from the road all count.
The Prophet forbade travelling to a hostile country carrying copies of the Quran.
At Khaibar the people flee to their fort as the Prophet cries Allahu Akbar, Khaibar is ruined; later his announcer forbids donkey meat and the pots are overturned.
Going up they said Allahu Akbar and going down Subhan Allah, told not to shout to One who hears and is near; returning, the Prophet said they return repentant, worshipping.
A slave who falls ill or travels is rewarded like the good deeds he did at home in health, as Abu Burda tells Yazid, who fasted on journeys.
At the Trench Az-Zubair volunteers three times to scout the enemy, and the Prophet says every prophet has a disciple and his is Az-Zubair.
If people knew what the Prophet knew, none would travel alone at night; he sped on open ground, delayed Maghrib to join Isha when hurrying, and urged travellers home quickly.
Umar wanted to buy back cheaply a horse he gave for Allah's Cause; the Prophet forbade it, likening one who takes back his gift to a dog swallowing its vomit.
A man asks to join jihad; learning his parents are alive, the Prophet tells him to exert himself in their service.
On one of his journeys the Prophet sent a messenger ordering that no string or other necklace be left round camels' necks.
No man may be alone with a woman, nor a woman travel without a mahram; a man enlisted for a campaign is told to go on Hajj with his wife.
Ali, Az-Zubair and Al-Miqdad take Hatib's letter to Meccan pagans from a woman; Hatib says he sought protection for his family, and the Prophet spares him as a Badr fighter.
Among the Badr prisoners Al-Abbas was undressed, so the Prophet clothed him in Abdullah bin Ubai's shirt, which is why he gave Abdullah his own shirt.
At Khaibar the Prophet cures Ali's eyes, gives him the flag and tells him to invite them calmly to Islam, as guiding one person is better than red camels.
Allah wonders at people who will enter Paradise in chains.
Three get a double reward: a man who teaches, frees and marries his slave girl, a Scripture believer who accepts the Prophet, and a faithful slave.
Asked about night raids endangering pagan women and children, the Prophet says they are from them; finding a woman killed in a campaign, he forbids killing women and children.
Withdrawing an order to burn two men, the Prophet says only Allah punishes with fire; Ibn Abbas says he would have killed, not burnt, the people Ali burnt.
Ukl men, healed by camels' milk and urine, kill the shepherd, take the camels and leave Islam; caught, they have hands and feet cut, eyes seared, and die without water.
An ant bit a prophet, who had its colony burnt, and Allah rebuked him for burning a whole nation that glorifies Allah because one ant bit him.
Sent by the Prophet, who prays for him to sit firm on horses, Jarir leads 150 Ahmas horsemen to dismantle and burn Dhul-Khalasa, an idol house called the Yemeni Ka'bah.
The Prophet burnt the date-palms of Bani An-Nadir.
The Prophet sends Ansar men against Abu Rafi; Abdullah bin Atik slips into his fort at night, kills him and, despite a sprained foot, waits to hear him mourned.
Do not wish to meet the enemy but be patient on meeting it, Paradise being under swords' shade; Khosrau and Caesar will be ruined; and war is deceit.
The Prophet seeks someone to kill Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf, who hurt Allah and His Apostle; allowed to say what he likes, Muhammad bin Maslama talks with Ka'b, then kills him.
Hiding behind palms to hear Ibn Saiyyad murmur under a sheet, the Prophet says that had his mother not alerted him, the truth would have been clear.
At the Trench the Prophet carries earth until dust covers his chest hair, loudly reciting Abdullah bin Rawaha's verses asking Allah for calm and firm feet against the enemy.
The Prophet always received Jarir with a smile, and when Jarir said he could not sit firm on horses, struck his chest and prayed he be firm and rightly guided.
Ali brought water in his shield, Fatima washed the blood from the Prophet's face, and ash from a burnt palm mat was put into his wound.
Sending Mu'adh and Abu Musa to Yemen, the Prophet tells them to make things easy, give glad tidings rather than drive people away, love each other and not differ.
At Uhud archers leave their post for booty against orders, seventy Muslims are killed, and the Prophet has Abu Sufyan's boasts of Hubal and Al-Uzza answered.
The Prophet was the most generous and bravest; when Medina took fright at night he rode Abu Talha's unsaddled horse with his sword, telling people not to be scared.
Salama bin Al-Akwa cries for help, chases off Ghatafan and Fazara raiders with arrows and recovers the Prophet's she-camels; the Prophet tells him to forgive them.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain but, attacked by the pagans, dismounted proclaiming himself the Prophet, son of Abdul Muttalib; none was braver that day.
When Bani Quraiza accept Sa'd's judgement, Sa'd rules that their warriors be killed and their women and children taken prisoner, and the Prophet says he judged as Allah judges.
Entering Mecca in the year of the Conquest wearing a helmet, the Prophet is told Ibn Khatal clings to the Ka'bah's curtains and orders him killed.
Ten scouts under Asim bin Thabit are surrounded by Bani Lihyan; Asim and six fall, Khubaib, sold in Mecca, prays two rak'at before being killed, and wasps guard Asim's body.
Free captives, feed the hungry, visit the sick; Ali's paper lists freeing captives; Al-Abbas's ransom is not waived; and a Badr captive hears the Prophet recite Surat at-Tur at Maghrib.
An infidel spy sits with the companions on a journey and leaves; at the Prophet's order Salama chases and kills him and is given the spy's belongings.
Stabbed, Umar urges his successor to keep the covenant with non-Muslims under Allah's and His Apostle's protection, fight to defend them and not tax them beyond their means.
Weeping, Ibn Abbas recalls the Thursday the Prophet's illness worsened: people disputed his call for writing materials, and he ordered the pagans expelled from Arabia and delegates honoured.
Umar urges buying a silk cloak for Eid and delegations; the Prophet says it is worn by one with no share in the Hereafter, yet sends Umar one to sell.
The Prophet tests young Ibn Saiyad and stops Umar killing him; later he warns that the Dajjal, of whom every prophet warned, is one-eyed, and Allah is not.
Asked on his Hajj where he will stay, the Prophet asks whether Aqil left them any house and names Khaif Bani Kinana, where Quraish swore to boycott Bani Hashim.
Umar tells his Hima manager not to oppress, to admit small herds but not those of the rich, and reserves the people's land only for mounts used in Allah's Cause.
Listing those who had professed Islam at the Prophet's order, the companions count 1,500 and wonder whether they need fear, yet later trials force some to pray alone in fear.
A man enlisted for a campaign whose wife is leaving for Hajj is told by the Prophet to go back and perform Hajj with her.
The Prophet calls a man claiming Islam one of the Fire; he fights fiercely, then kills himself when wounded, and the Prophet announces that only a Muslim enters Paradise.
Weeping, the Prophet announces Zaid, Ja'far and Abdullah bin Rawaha martyred before Khalid took the flag unappointed and was given victory; seventy Ansar are betrayed and killed at Bi'r Ma'una.
After conquering a people the Prophet stayed three days in their town, and he set out for Umrah from Al-Ji'rana, where he shared out the Hunain booty.
Ibn Umar's horse and runaway slave, lost to the enemy and the Byzantines, are returned to him once the Muslims win, Khalid bin Al-Walid restoring them.
Jabir invites the Prophet and a few others to a young sheep and a Sa of barley, but the Prophet loudly calls the people of the Trench to come.
The Prophet praises Um Khalid's yellow shirt in Ethiopian, lets her play with the seal of prophethood, and three times wishes her to wear it out, and she lived long.
When Al-Hasan bin Ali puts a charity date in his mouth, the Prophet stops him in Persian, saying they do not eat charity.
The Prophet calls Ghulul a great sin whose doers bear animals, gold or clothes on their necks at Resurrection, beyond his intercession; Karkara, who stole booty, is in the Fire.
Pots cooked before the booty's division are overturned; ten sheep count as a camel; a runaway camel may be shot; and any blood-letting tool but tooth or nail may slaughter.
Jarir, for whom the Prophet prayed to sit firm, leads 150 Ahmas riders to dismantle and burn Dhul-Khalasa, the Yemeni Ka'bah, and the Prophet blesses them five times.
No migration remains after the Conquest of Mecca, only jihad and good intention; the Prophet takes Mujalid's pledge for Islam instead, and Aisha says the same.
Ali recounts seizing Hatib's letter and the Prophet excusing him as a Badr warrior, words a supporter of Uthman says emboldened Ali to shed blood.
Boys meet the returning Prophet, who says 'we return repentant', is aided by Abu Talha when his camel slips with Safiya, and prays two rak'at in the mosque.
Ali's two she-camels, from his Badr booty and the Khumus, are mutilated by Hamza drinking with Ansari men; the Prophet rebukes him, but seeing him drunk, withdraws.
Abu Bakr refuses Fatima her inheritance from the Prophet's Fai, as prophets leave only charity; Umar, judging Ali and Abbas, explains how the Prophet and his successors managed that property.
The Abdul Qais delegation are told to believe in Allah, pray, pay zakat, fast Ramadan and pay a fifth of booty, and are forbidden four vessels used for alcoholic drinks.
The Prophet's heirs take no Dinar, all beyond his wives' and workers' expenses being charity; he left some barley in Aisha's house, his arms, a white mule and charity land.
In his last illness the Prophet is nursed in Aisha's house with his wives' leave, and dies there leaning on her chest after she softens a siwak for him.
Walking Safiya back from his I'tikaf, the Prophet tells two passing Ansari men she is his wife, as Satan circulates in people like blood and might plant suspicion.
Ibn Umar saw the Prophet in Hafsa's house relieving himself with his back to the Qibla, facing Sham.
The Prophet prayed Asr while the sun still shone in Aisha's dwelling.
In a sermon the Prophet points toward Aisha's house, eastward, saying three times that affliction will come from there, where the side of Satan's head appears.
Hearing a man ask to enter Hafsa's house, the Prophet says he is her foster uncle, as whatever blood relations forbid, foster relations forbid too.
The Prophet's ring, engraved Muhammad Apostle Allah, seals Abu Bakr's letter; Anas shows his worn shoes, Aisha the patched garment he died in, and his cup is mended with silver.
Al-Miswar, offering to guard the Prophet's sword, recalls his sermon when Ali sought Abu Jahl's daughter: Fatima is from him, and the two cannot be one man's wives.
Ali sends his son with a document of the Prophet's rules on charity to Uthman for his Zakat officials, and Uthman declines it.
Instead of a servant from booty slave girls, the Prophet teaches Fatima and Ali bedtime words: Allahu Akbar 34 times, Al-hamdu lillah and Subhan Allah 33 each.
People may name sons after the Prophet but not use his kunya, for he is Qasim, the distributor; he praises the Ansar for refusing that title to a boy's father.
Allah gives religious understanding to whom He wills good; He is the Giver and the Prophet only the distributor, giving as ordered, and this nation stays victorious.
Some people spend Allah's wealth unjustly, and they will be put in the Fire on the Day of Resurrection.
Horses bring reward and booty; Khosrau's and Caesar's treasures will be spent for Allah; booty, consumed by fire for an earlier prophet, is lawful now; Umar keeps conquered land undivided.
Asked whether fighting for booty, fame or to show bravery is in Allah's Cause, the Prophet says only fighting so that Allah's Word is superior is.
The Prophet keeps a gifted silk cloak for Makhrama and brings it to him; once Quraiza and An-Nadir are conquered, he repays those who gave him date-palms.
At Al-Jamal Az-Zubair asks his son to pay his debts, seeking Allah's help; Abdullah sells property, settles 2.2 million, calls claimants for four Hajj seasons, then divides the estate.
Uthman missed Badr to tend his ill wife, the Prophet's daughter, and the Prophet promised him the reward and share of one who fought there.
The Hawazin, now Muslim, ask back their property and captives; told to choose one, they choose captives, and the Muslims willingly return them, as their leaders confirm to the Prophet.
Abu Musa recalls the Prophet swearing to give them no mounts, then giving them booty camels: if something else proves better, he does it and expiates his oath.
A Najd raiding party got eleven or twelve camels each and one extra, the Prophet giving some members extra shares; Abu Musa's shipmates from Ethiopia shared Khaibar's booty without fighting.
When Bahrain's wealth arrives after the Prophet's death, Abu Bakr honours his promises, giving Jabir handfuls of money, and answers his charge of miserliness.
Told to be just while distributing booty at Al-Ji'rana, the Prophet replies he would be miserable if he did not act justly.
The Prophet says that had Al-Mut'im bin Adi lived and interceded for the Badr prisoners, he would have freed them for his sake.
The Prophet gives Bani Al-Muttalib a share but not Bani Abd Shams or Naufal, telling Jubair and Uthman that Bani Al-Muttalib and Bani Hashim are one.
At Badr two Ansari youths kill Abu Jahl, his spoils going to Mu'adh bin Amr; at Hunain Abu Qatada gets the spoils of the pagan he killed.
The Prophet tells Hakim that wealth taken without greed is blessed and the giving hand is better, so Hakim never again accepts anything, even from Abu Bakr and Umar.
Umar, told to fulfil a pre-Islamic I'tikaf vow, frees his two slave girls from the Hunain captives when the Prophet frees those captives without ransom.
The Prophet gives to some to hold them to Islam, reassures the Ansar over the Hawazin booty, gives to grabbing bedouins, and bears a charge of injustice like Moses.
Asma carried date stones from land the Prophet gave Az-Zubair, land taken from the property of Bani An-Nadir.
The Prophet let Khaibar's Jews work its land for half the fruit as long as he wished; Umar later expelled them, and all Jews and Christians, from Hijaz.
At Khaibar a man grabs a thrown container of fat, booty honey and grapes are eaten not stored, and the Prophet has pots of donkey meat overturned.
Umar orders close-kin marriages among Magians annulled, and takes jizya from Magians only after Abdur-Rahman bin Auf testifies the Prophet took it from the Magians of Hajar.
As Abu Ubaida brings Bahrain's jizya, the Prophet tells the Ansar he fears not their poverty but luxury, over which they will compete and be destroyed like past nations.
Advised by Al-Hurmuzan to strike Khosrau first, Umar sends An-Nu'man; Al-Mughira tells Khosrau's envoy their Prophet ordered them to fight until they worship Allah alone or pay jizya.
Umar sends Muslims against Khosrau; al-Mughira tells Khosrau's envoy the Prophet ordered them to fight until Allah alone is worshipped or Jizya paid, and an-Nu'man waits till midday.
At Tabuk the Prophet gives Aila's king, who sent him a mule and cloak, a treaty keeping his authority; Umar urges keeping Allah's covenant with the Dhimmis, the Prophet's convention.
Offered land in Bahrain, the Ansar refuse unless their Quraishi brothers get the same, and the Prophet tells them to be patient with the preference they will see after him.
Abu Bakr pays Jabir what the Prophet promised him from Bahrain's revenue; the Prophet distributes Bahrain's money in the mosque till none remains, refusing to help al-Abbas lift his share.
Whoever kills a person who has a treaty with the Muslims will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though it can be perceived from forty years' distance.
At Bait-ul-Midras the Prophet tells the Jews they will be safe if they embrace Islam, that he wants to expel them, and that they may sell their property.
Ibn Abbas weeps recalling Thursday, when the gravely ill Prophet asked for a scapula to write on, people disputed, and he ordered pagans expelled from Arabia and delegates given gifts.
After Khaibar's conquest the Prophet questions the Jews about a poisoned sheep given him; they admit poisoning it to learn whether he was a liar or a prophet.
Anas says Qunut is before bowing; the Prophet invoked evil on Bani Sulaim for a month, and grieved most for the Qaris whom pagans killed despite a peace pact.
The Prophet honours the asylum Um Hani gave a man on the day Mecca was conquered, and Ali's paper says any Muslim's asylum binds all and declares Medina a sanctuary.
Abdullah bin Sahl is found murdered in Khaibar, then under treaty; his kin cannot swear to the killer and reject the Jews' oaths, so the Prophet pays the blood money.
Heraclius summoned Abu Sufyan and a Quraishi trading caravan in Sham during the truce the Prophet had concluded with Abu Sufyan and the Quraish infidels.
The Prophet was once bewitched, so that he imagined he had done things he had not done.
At Tabuk the Prophet names six signs before the Hour: his death, Jerusalem's conquest, a plague, overflowing wealth, an affliction in every Arab house, and Byzantine betrayal after a truce.
On the day of Nahr Abu Bakr has it announced that no pagan may perform Hajj after that year nor anyone circle the Ka'ba naked, throwing back the pagans' covenant.
Lying, breaking promises, treachery in covenants and abuse in quarrels make a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up.
Ali says they wrote only the Quran and a paper from the Prophet: Medina is a sanctuary, even the lowest Muslim's asylum binds all, and its betrayer is cursed.
Abu Huraira foretells, from the Prophet, a time when Allah and His Apostle's asylum for the Dhimmis is outraged, and Allah makes them dare to refuse the Jizya.
At Siffin Sahl bin Hunaif recalls Hudaibiya, when Umar protested the terms to the Prophet and Abu Bakr, and after Surat al-Fath the Prophet told him it was a victory.
During the Quraish peace treaty Asma's pagan mother visits her hoping for a reward from her, and the Prophet tells Asma to keep good relations with her.
Before an Umrah the Meccans allow the Prophet three days with sheathed arms; he erases 'Apostle of Allah' from the treaty himself when Ali refuses, and leaves after three days.
When Uqba throws camel intestines on the prostrating Prophet, he invokes Allah against the Quraish chiefs he names, later all killed at Badr and thrown into a well.
Every betrayer will have a flag on the Day of Resurrection, fixed or shown so that he is recognised and his betrayal made known.
Conquering Mecca, the Prophet says there is no migration now, only Jihad and intention, and Mecca is a sanctuary whose plants and game are protected, except Idhkhir.
The Prophet tells Yemenis that first there was only Allah, His Throne over the water, then heavens and earth were created; once he described creation through to Paradise and Hell.
Allah says the son of Adam slights Him by claiming He has a son and disbelieves in Him by denying He will recreate him as He first created him.
When Allah completed creation, He wrote in His Book with Him on His Throne: 'My Mercy overpowers My Anger'.
Whoever unjustly takes even a span of land will have it encircling his neck down seven earths, or sink down the seven earths on the Day of Resurrection.
Time has returned to its form at the creation of heavens and earth: the year has twelve months, four sacred, Dhul-Qa'da, Dhul-Hijja and Muharram in succession, and Mudar's Rajab.
Sued by Arwa before Marwan, Sa'id bin Zaid denies wronging her, citing the Prophet: whoever unjustly takes a span of land will have it round his neck down seven earths.
The sun prostrates beneath the Throne and asks leave to rise, until told to rise in the west; the sun and moon will be folded up on Resurrection Day.
The sun and moon are two of Allah's signs, not eclipsed for anyone's death or life, so pray at eclipses; the Prophet prayed two long rak'at, each with two bowings.
The Prophet was granted victory by the easterly wind and 'Ad destroyed by the westerly; clouds made him anxious until rain fell, lest they bring a tormenting wind.

His body opened and washed with Zamzam, the Prophet rides Al-Buraq with Gabriel through seven heavens greeting prophets, sees Al-Bait-al-Ma'mur and Sidrat-ul-Muntaha, and fifty prayers are reduced to five.
Formed in the womb in forty-day stages, each person has an angel write his deeds, livelihood, death and whether blessed or wretched, and what is written decides his final deeds.
Gabriel announces in heaven whom Allah loves; angels talk in the clouds as devils eavesdrop for soothsayers, record Friday arrivals at the mosque, and Gabriel supports Hassan's verses.
Asked how revelation comes, the Prophet says the angel sometimes comes like a ringing bell, the hardest on him, and sometimes in a man's form and speaks to him.
Whoever spends a pair of things in Allah's cause will be called by Paradise's gatekeepers, and the Prophet hopes Abu Bakr will be among them.
Gabriel greets Aisha, descends only by Allah's order, reads the Quran in seven ways, leads five prayers and says those dying without associating others enter Paradise; angels come in shifts.
Angels do not enter a house with pictures or a dog; picture-makers will be punished, the Prophet tells Aisha over a pictured pillow; Zaid excepts embroidery on garments.
Angels pray for those awaiting prayer; Malik keeps Hell; the Prophet declines the Angel of the Mountains' offer to crush his people, and saw Gabriel's real form with 600 wings.
A wife who refuses her husband's call to bed, so that he sleeps angry, is cursed by the angels till morning.
After a pause in revelation the Prophet saw the Hira angel seated between sky and earth, fell down, asked his family to cover him, and 'O you wrapped up' came.
On the night of his Ascent the Prophet saw tall brown Moses, medium-height Jesus, Malik the keeper of Hell and the Dajjal; angels will guard Medina from the Dajjal.
After death each person is shown his place in Paradise or Hell morning and evening; the Prophet saw the poor most numerous in Paradise and women most numerous in Hell.
The Prophet dreams of Umar's palace in Paradise; its tents are hollow pearls, its joys beyond imagining, its first entrants shine like the full moon, and Sa'd's handkerchiefs surpass silk.
A lash's space in Paradise outweighs the world; one tree's shade outlasts a century's ride; it has lofty mansions, a wet-nurse for Ibrahim, and Ar-Raiyan gate for the fasting.
Hell's breaths cause severe heat and cold, and fever is from its heat; its fire is seventy times ours, and one who enjoined good but did evil circles in it.
Bewitched, the Prophet learns in a dream that Labid bin Al-A'sam worked the magic with a comb and hair placed in Dharwan's well, and Allah cures him.
Satan knots sleepers' heads, urinates in a late sleeper's ear, prompts 'who created your Lord?' and runs in people like blood; Allah's name and Ayat al-Kursi keep him away.
Satan flees the adhan, distracts the praying, touches newborns except Jesus, brings yawning and bad dreams, set Muslims against Muslims at Uhud, avoids Umar's path and lodges in noses overnight.
Raise your voice in the adhan, Abu Sa'id tells a man fond of sheep and desert, for every human, jinn or thing hearing it will testify for him.
The Prophet ordered snakes killed, especially those with two white lines or a short tail, which blind and cause abortion, but later forbade killing snakes living in houses.
A time will come when a man's best property is sheep he grazes on mountain tops and rain-fed pastures, fleeing with his religion from afflictions.
Disbelief's source is in the east and pride among camel and horse owners, gentleness among sheep owners; belief is Yemenite, harshness among Rabi'a and Mudar where Satan's two horns appear.
Roosters crow on seeing an angel, so ask Allah's blessing; donkeys bray on seeing Satan, so seek refuge; at nightfall keep children close and shut doors, which Satan cannot open.
A lost group of Israelites were, the Prophet thinks, cursed and changed into rats, since rats refuse she-camel milk but drink sheep's milk.
Salamanders and snakes with two white lines or short tails are ordered killed, house snakes spared; five harmful animals, rats included, may be killed in the Sanctuary or Ihram.
A woman entered Hell for starving a cat, a prostitute was forgiven for watering a dog, a prophet was rebuked for burning ants, and needless dogs cost a Qirat daily.
Allah created Adam sixty cubits tall and sent him to greet the angels, whose reply became his offspring's greeting; Paradise's people will have his form, and people have shrunk since.
Um Sulaim asks whether a woman must bathe after a wet dream, and the Prophet says yes if she sees discharge, which explains why a child resembles its mother.
Abdullah bin Salam asks three things only a prophet knows, accepts Islam on the answers, and the Jews, who had called him their best, then call him their worst.
But for Israelites meat would not decay, and but for Eve wives would not betray husbands; treat women kindly, for woman is created from a rib that breaks if straightened.
In the womb an angel records a person's deeds, death, livelihood and whether wretched or blessed, and what is written decides whether his last deeds lead to Paradise or Fire.
Allah will ask the least-punished in the Fire if he would ransom himself with the earth, reminding him that in Adam's backbone He asked less: to worship none besides Him.
Every unjust murder carries a share of guilt for Adam's first son, who began the practice of murder.
Souls are like recruited troops: those of similar qualities incline to one another, and those of dissimilar qualities differ.
Every prophet, Noah among them, warned his nation of the Dajjal, but the Prophet adds that he is one-eyed, unlike Allah, and his Paradise will really be Hell.
On Resurrection Day Noah's nation will deny he conveyed the message, and Muhammad and his followers will bear witness for him, explaining the verse on being a just nation.
At a meal the Prophet says on Resurrection Day people will seek intercession from Adam and Noah, who decline, then come to him, and he will prostrate beneath the Throne.
The Prophet recited the verse 'Fahal min Muddakir' in the usual way.
Gabriel opens the Prophet's chest, washes it with Zamzam and takes him up the heavens past Adam, Idris, Moses, Jesus and Abraham; fifty prayers become five, then he enters Paradise.
The Prophet says he was granted victory by the easterly wind As-Saba, while the people of 'Ad were destroyed by the westerly wind Ad-Dabur.
A man rebukes the Prophet for giving Ali's gold to four chiefs; the Prophet foretells among his offspring Quran reciters who leave the religion like an arrow and kill Muslims.
Abdullah heard the Prophet recite 'Fahal min Muddakir'.
Alarmed, the Prophet says an opening has been made in Gog and Magog's wall, warns the Arabs, and says they will perish, despite pious among them, when evil increases.
Adam will be told to bring out 999 of every thousand for the Fire; people are gathered barefoot and naked, Abraham clothed first, and some companions taken to the Fire.
Abraham's plea for his father Azar on Resurrection Day is refused, Paradise being forbidden to disbelievers; the Prophet condemns Ka'ba pictures showing Abraham and Ishmael divining with arrows.
Asked who is most honourable, the Prophet says the most righteous, then Joseph, a prophet son of prophets, and among Arabs those best before Islam, if they understand religion.
Abraham, tall in the Prophet's dream and resembling him, circumcised himself at eighty and lied only thrice, once shielding Sarah from a tyrant; a salamander blew the fire on him.
The 'wrong' that must not be mixed with belief in verse 6.83 means joining others with Allah, the Prophet tells worried companions, citing Luqman's advice to his son.
On Resurrection Day people gathered on one plain will ask Abraham to intercede, but remembering his lies he says 'Myself!' and sends them to Moses.
Abraham leaves Ishmael and his mother near the Ka'ba; she runs between Safa and Marwa, an angel brings forth Zamzam, Jurhum settle, and Abraham and Ishmael build the Ka'ba.
The first mosque built on earth was al-Masjid al-Haram, then al-Aqsa forty years later, and wherever prayer time comes one should pray there.
Seeing Uhud, the Prophet says it loves us and we love it, and declares the area between Medina's two mountains a sanctuary, as Abraham made Mecca one.
The Prophet tells Aisha her people built the Ka'ba short of Abraham's foundations, and he would rebuild it but that they had only recently left disbelief.
Asked how to send blessings on him, the Prophet teaches asking Allah to bless Muhammad and his family as He blessed Abraham and Abraham's family.
The Prophet sought refuge for Al-Hasan and Al-Husain with Abraham's words for Ishmael and Isaac: Allah's perfect words against every devil, poisonous pest and evil eye.
The Prophet says we would doubt sooner than Abraham, who asked to see the dead revived; he asks mercy on Lot, and would have accepted release after Joseph's long imprisonment.
Finding men of Aslam at archery, the Prophet urges the offspring of Ishmael to shoot, as their father was an archer, and says he is with both teams.
Asked who is most honourable, the Prophet says the most Allah-fearing, then Joseph, a prophet son of prophets, and among Arabs those best before Islam, if they understand religion.
The Prophet asks Allah to forgive Lot, who wanted to have a powerful support.
The Prophet recited the verse 'Hal min Muddakir', is there any that will remember.
Salih's she-camel was hamstrung by a man of honour and power; at Thamud's Al-Hijr the Prophet has its well water poured out and forbids entering the wrongdoers' homes except weeping.
Joseph is the honourable son of the honourable Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham; asked who is most honourable, the Prophet names the most Allah-fearing, then Joseph.
In his illness the Prophet insists Abu Bakr lead the prayer despite Aisha's plea that he is soft-hearted, likening her to Joseph's female companions, and Abu Bakr leads.
The Prophet prays for the rescue of Aiyyash and Salama bin Hisham and asks Allah to punish Mudar with years of drought like those in Joseph's time.
The Prophet asks Allah's mercy on Lot, who wanted powerful support, and says that after a stay in prison as long as Joseph's he would have accepted release.
Told of the story spread about her, Aisha faints and wakes with fever, likening her case to Jacob's with his sons, until verses come and she thanks only Allah.
Aisha explains verse 12.110: the apostles despaired of their disbelieving nations and feared even their followers wavered, never doubting their Lord, until Allah's help came.
Joseph, son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, is the honourable son of honourable fathers.
Job, bathing, gathered falling gold locusts, and when his Lord asked whether He had not made him rich enough, said he could never do without His blessing.
Returning to Khadija with a pounding heart, the Prophet is taken to Waraqa, a Christian reader of the Gospels, who says it was the angel Allah sent to Moses.
The Prophet says none should call him better than Jonah, and recounts his Night Journey: Aaron in the fifth heaven, Moses and Jesus described, and milk chosen over wine.
Finding Medina's Jews fasting Ashura for the day Allah saved Moses and drowned Pharaoh's folk, the Prophet says he is closer to Moses, fasts it and orders Muslims to fast.
When people fall unconscious on Resurrection Day, the Prophet, first to recover, will see Moses holding a pillar of the Throne, perhaps spared for his swoon at the Tur.
Were it not for the Children of Israel meat would not decay, and were it not for Eve no woman would betray her husband.
Moses, saying none is more learned, seeks Al-Khadir where the fish is lost but cannot stay patient as Khadir holes a boat, kills a boy and mends a wall.
Bani Israel change 'Repentance' at the gate; Moses, said to hide a defect, is cleared when a stone runs off with his clothes, and he bore worse harm patiently.
Picking Arak fruit, the Prophet says the black ones are best, and when asked if he had been a shepherd, says every prophet was one.
Moses slaps the Angel of Death, is offered a year for each hair under his hand on an ox, but chooses death now near the Sacred Land.
The Prophet forbids preferring him over Moses, whom he will see holding Allah's Throne at the Resurrection; Adam answers Moses' blame with his written fate; Moses' followers fill a horizon.
Of women only Asia, Pharaoh's wife, and Mary, daughter of Imran, reached perfection, and Aisha excels other women as tharid excels other meals.
None should say the Prophet is better than Jonah bin Matta; angered when an Ansari slapped a Jew over Moses, he forbade ranking Allah's prophets above one another.
Reciting the Psalms was made easy for David, who ate only from his own labour; his fasting on alternate days and his night prayer are the most beloved to Allah.
Asked about prostrating at Surat Sad, Ibn Abbas cites the verse telling the Prophet to follow David, Solomon and earlier prophets; it is not compulsory, though the Prophet prostrated.
The Prophet freed a demon he caught, recalling Solomon's prayer for a unique kingdom; Solomon, not saying 'If Allah will' over seventy women, had only a half child born.
Al-Masjid al-Haram was the first mosque built and Al-Aqsa the next, forty years apart, and wherever prayer time comes the whole earth is a place of prayer.
The Prophet likens himself and people to a man whose fire draws moths, and tells how Solomon gave a child two women disputed to the younger, reversing David.
When companions feared the verse on mixing belief with wrong, the Prophet explained that wrong as joining others in worship with Allah, citing Luqman's advice to his son.
On the night of his Ascension the Prophet met John and Jesus, cousins, in the second heaven, and they welcomed him as a pious brother and pious prophet.
Satan touches every newborn but Mary and her son; Mary is named with Khadija as best of women and with Asia as perfect; Quraish women are best of camel-riding women.
Whoever testifies that none but Allah may be worshipped, that Muhammad and Jesus are His slaves and apostles, Jesus His Word and spirit, and Paradise and Hell true, enters Paradise.
Three spoke in the cradle: Jesus, a baby who cleared the Israelite Juraij of a false charge, and an infant who preferred a falsely accused slave girl to a tyrant.
The Prophet describes Moses, Jesus and Abraham as seen on the night of his Ascension, when he chose milk over wine and was told he had taken the right path.
In a dream at the Ka'bah the Prophet saw Jesus circling it, brown with lank dripping hair, and behind him the Dajjal, curly-haired and blind in the right eye.
The Prophet is nearest to Jesus, prophets sharing one religion; Jesus believed a thief's oath; do not overpraise the Prophet as Christians did Jesus; believers in both get double reward.
People will be resurrected barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, Abraham clothed first; some companions will be taken aside as renegades, and the Prophet will answer in the words of Jesus.
The son of Mary will descend as a just ruler, breaking the cross, killing pigs and ending the jizya, when wealth is so plentiful that nobody accepts it.
The Dajjal's fire will be cool water; among earlier people Allah forgave a man who eased his debtors and another who had his body burnt out of fear of Him.
On his deathbed the Prophet invoked Allah's curse on the Jews and Christians for building places of worship at their prophets' graves, warning Muslims against doing so.
Prophets ruled the Israelites one after another, but after the Prophet will come caliphs: obey the first given the pledge and give them their rights, for Allah will question them.
Muslims will follow Jews' and Christians' ways; the adhan and a prayer posture differ from theirs; a parable gives Muslims double wages; Jews are cursed for selling forbidden fat.
Convey the Prophet's teaching even one sentence; telling stories of the Children of Israel is no sin; whoever deliberately lies about the Prophet takes his place in the Fire.
The Jews and Christians do not dye their grey hair, so Muslims are told to do the opposite.
Among earlier peoples a suicide was denied Paradise, three Israelites were tested with health and wealth, three trapped in a cave were freed by sincere deeds, and a baby spoke.
An Israelite prostitute took off her shoe to water a dog dying of thirst, and Allah forgave her for it.
Holding a tuft of hair, Muawiya said the Prophet forbade false hair, saying the Israelites were destroyed when their women used it.
Among earlier peoples were persons inspired with what came true, and if the Prophet's followers have any, it is Umar bin Al-Khattab.
An Israelite who had murdered ninety-nine was forgiven dying on his way to repent; a cow and a wolf spoke; land buyer and seller each refused gold found buried there.
Plague was a punishment on Israelites or earlier people and a mercy for believers: do not enter or flee a plague land, and one staying patiently gets a martyr's reward.
Rebuking Usama's intercession for a Makhzumi woman who stole, the Prophet said earlier nations perished by sparing nobles, and he would cut off even Fatima's hand if she stole.
Two men recited a verse differently; displeased at their dispute, the Prophet said both were correct and they should not differ, for nations before them differed and were destroyed.
The Prophet told of a prophet whose people beat him bloody, who wiped his face saying: O Allah, forgive my nation, for they have no knowledge.
Allah forgave men who, fearing Him, had their bodies burnt and scattered after death, and a lender who told his servant to forgive poor debtors so Allah might forgive them.
A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she imprisoned until it died, neither feeding it nor setting it free to find food.
Among the sayings of earlier prophets that people still have: if you do not feel ashamed, then do whatever you like.
A man walking in pride with his garment dragging was swallowed by the earth and will go on sinking in it until the Day of Resurrection.
Muslims, last to come, will be foremost at the Resurrection; earlier nations differed over Friday, Saturday going to the Jews and Sunday to the Christians; Muslims must bathe weekly.
On his last visit to Medina Muawiya showed a tuft of false hair in a sermon, saying the Prophet called the practice falsehood.
Ibn Abbas explains that in verse 49.13 Shu'ub means the large nations and Qabail the branch tribes.
Asked who is the most honourable of people, the Prophet said the most righteous, and when they said that was not their question, Joseph, the prophet of Allah.
Zainab bint Abi Salama confirms that the Prophet was of the tribe of Mudar, descended from An-Nadr bin Kinana, and reports his ban on four kinds of wine vessels.
People differ in nature: the best before Islam are the best in Islam if they understand religion, the best hate ruling most, and the worst is the double-faced.
Quraish lead in ruling, Muslims following their Muslims and disbelievers their disbelievers; the best hate ruling; Ibn Abbas says verse 42.23 asks Quraish to keep their kinship with the Prophet.
Afflictions come from the east; rudeness and pride mark the camel-herding bedouins of Rabi'a and Mudar, calmness the owners of sheep, while belief and wisdom are Yemenite.
Angered at talk of a king from Qahtan, Muawiya cited the Prophet: ruling stays with Quraish while they keep the religion; another report adds, even if only two remain.
The Prophet told Uthman that Bani Hashim and Bani Al-Muttalib are one, and Aisha treated women of Bani Zuhra kindly for their relation to the Prophet.
Quraish, the Ansar, Juhaina, Muzaina, Aslam, Ashja' and Ghifar are the Prophet's disciples, with no protector except Allah and His Apostle.
Aisha vowed never to speak to Abdullah bin Az-Zubair for wanting to stop her charity; the Prophet's Zuhri uncles won her over, and she freed forty slaves in expiation.
Uthman had Zaid bin Thabit and three Quraishis copy the Quran, telling them to write in the language of Quraish where they differed, as it was revealed in it.
Passing men of Aslam at archery, the Prophet told the children of Ishmael to shoot, their father being an archer, and said he was with both teams.
Knowingly claiming a false father is disbelief and a false people earns the Fire; such claims, invented dreams and sayings falsely ascribed to the Prophet are among the worst lies.
The Abd al-Qais delegation of Rabi'a, cut off by Mudar's disbelievers, are told to believe in Allah, pray, pay Zakat, give a fifth of booty and avoid four vessels.
From the pulpit the Prophet pointed east, saying afflictions will start from there, where the side of Satan's head comes out.
Quraish, the Ansar, Juhaina, Muzaina, Aslam, Ghifar and Ashja' are the Prophet's helpers; he prayed for Ghifar and Aslam and ranked them above Tamim, Asad, Ghatafan and Amir.
The Hour will not be established until a man from Qahtan appears, driving the people with his stick.
The Prophet condemned the call of Ignorance when an emigrant and Ansari quarrelled, refused to kill Ibn Ubai, and disowned whoever slaps his face, tears his dress or so calls.
Amr bin Luhai, father of Khuza'a, was seen dragging his intestines in the Fire as the first to free animals for false gods, and the Bahira and Saiba are explained.
Abu Dhar of Ghifar tells how Ali secretly led him to the Prophet in Mecca, where he embraced Islam and was twice beaten for declaring it, Al-Abbas shielding him.
Aslam, Ghifar and some of Muzaina and Juhaina are better with Allah than the tribes of Asad, Tamim, Hawazin and Ghatafan.
Ibn Abbas points to the verses after 6.130, on those who killed their children in folly and forbade what Allah provided, to show the ignorance of the Arabs.
When told to warn his near kindred, the Prophet called each tribe of Quraish by name, telling Bani Abd Manaf, his aunt and Fatima to buy themselves from Allah.
Asking the Ansar whether any stranger was among them, the Prophet said the son of a people's sister belongs to them.
During the days of Mina the Prophet stopped Abu Bakr rebuking two girls beating drums, as these were Eid days, and let Ethiopians play in the mosque while Aisha watched.
Seeking to satirise the infidels, Hassan bin Thabit would draw the Prophet out of their lineage like a hair from dough; Aisha forbade abusing him, for he defended the Prophet.
The Prophet's five names include Al-Mahi, Al-Hashir and Al-Aqib, no prophet after him; Quraish curse Mudhammam, not Muhammad; he is the last brick completing the prophets' house.
Aisha said the Prophet died when he was sixty-three years old.
People may name themselves after the Prophet but not use his kunya, as he said when a man in the market called out Abu-l-Qasim.
Strong at ninety-four, As-Sa'ib bin Yazid credits his hearing and sight to the Prophet's prayer for him when sick, and he saw the seal between the Prophet's shoulders.
Al-Hasan resembled the Prophet; companions describe him as of medium height, rosy, handsome and moon-faced, with few white hairs, his hand colder than ice and more fragrant than musk.
The Prophet was most generous in Ramadan, beamed when happy, chose the easier course, took revenge only for Allah, was shy, and never spoke obscenely or faulted food.
The Prophet's armpits showed in prostration and rain prayer, his words could be counted, he prayed no more than eleven rak'at, and his eyes slept but not his heart.
A woman's two waterskins served forty men, water flowed from the Prophet's fingers for hundreds, Hudaybiyyah's drained well refilled, small meals fed many, and Jabir's dates paid his father's debts.
In a Friday sermon during drought the Prophet raised his hands for rain, which fell all week until he asked for it around Medina and not on it.
When the Prophet moved to a new pulpit, the palm trunk he had preached beside cried like a child until he came and put his hand on it.
Hudhaifa told Umar that the afflictions surging like waves lay behind a closed door that would be broken, and later said the door was Umar.
Before the Hour Muslims will fight the Turks and others with small eyes, red flat-nosed faces like shields and hairy shoes; the best people hate ruling until chosen for it.
Muslims fighting the Jews will be given victory, a stone telling a Muslim to kill a Jew behind it; holy wars are won while companions, then their companions, are present.
The Prophet foretold Adi a woman's safe journey from Al-Hira to the Ka'bah and Khosrau's treasures taken, which Adi saw, and urged shielding oneself from Hell with half a date.
After praying for Uhud's martyrs, the Prophet said he sees his Fount and holds the world's treasure keys, and fears not polytheism for them but rivalry for worldly things.
From a high building in Medina the Prophet said he saw afflictions falling among their houses like raindrops.
In fear the Prophet told Zainab bint Jahsh a hole had opened in the wall of Gog and Magog, and that they would perish, pious among them, if evil increased.
In afflictions sitting beats running and sheep taken to hilltops are the best property; give rights when others are preferred; Quraish youths will ruin people; Hudhaifa asks about evil ahead.
The Hour will not come until two groups with one claim fight with great casualties, and about thirty liars appear, each claiming to be Allah's messenger.
Sparing Dhul-Khuwaisira who demanded justice, the Prophet foretold people whose Quran does not pass their throats, who leave Islam like an arrow; Ali fought them and found the man described.
To companions complaining of persecution, the Prophet recalled earlier believers sawn apart and combed with iron who kept their religion, and said Islam will prevail, but they are hasty.
Thabit bin Qais, fearing his voice raised over the Prophet's had annulled his deeds, was told that he is of the people of Paradise, not of the Fire.
A cloud hovered over a man reciting Surat al-Kahf as his animal took fright, and the Prophet said it was peace descending for the recitation of the Quran.
On the Migration Abu Bakr made the Prophet a bed in the shade and brought him a shepherd's milk; Suraqa's horse sank until he promised to turn back pursuers.
Visiting a sick bedouin, the Prophet wished him a cure; when the man said his fever would take him to the grave, he replied: may it be as you say.
A Christian convert who wrote for the Prophet returned to Christianity, saying the Prophet knew only what he wrote; three times the earth threw out his body after burial.
When Khosrau perishes there will be no Khosrau after him, nor Caesar after Caesar, and their treasures will be spent in Allah's Cause.
The Prophet refused Musailama even a palm leaf and read two gold bracelets in a dream as two liars; another dream showed migration to Medina, a broken sword and cows.
The Prophet told Fatima he would die, and she, first of his family, would follow him; Ibn Abbas read Surah 110 as foretelling it; his last address commended the Ansar.
Taking Al-Hasan up the pulpit, the Prophet called him a chief through whom he hoped Allah would reconcile two Muslim groups.
The Prophet announced Ja'far's and Zaid's deaths before the news came and foretold Jabir's carpets; Umaiya, told the Prophet would kill him, went to Badr and was killed.
In a dream the Prophet saw Abu Bakr draw one or two weak buckets from a well, then Umar draw so strongly that all the people drank their fill.
Gabriel talked with the Prophet while Um Salama was present, and she took him for Dihya until she heard the Prophet speak of Gabriel in his sermon.
When Jews claimed the Torah only ordered lashing for a man and woman guilty of illegal intercourse, Abdullah bin Salam exposed the stoning verse, and the Prophet ordered both stoned.
In the Prophet's lifetime the moon split in two when the Meccans asked for a miracle, and two companions walking on a dark night were lit by two lamp-like lights.
A group of the Prophet's followers will remain obedient to Allah's orders and victorious, unharmed by those who oppose them, until the Last Day comes.
Blessed by the Prophet, Urwa profited in every deal; goodness is in horses until the Resurrection, a horse bringing reward, a living or sin according to why it is kept.
Reaching Khaybar in the early morning, the Prophet saw its people flee to their fort and said: Allah is Greater, Khaybar is ruined.
Abu Huraira, who forgot many narrations, spread his sheet as the Prophet told him, wrapped himself in what the Prophet scooped into it, and never forgot again.
Holy wars are won with a companion present, later a companion's companion, then theirs; the best are the Prophet's generation and the next, then come false witnesses.
Fleeing Mecca, Abu Bakr made the Prophet a bed in the shade and brought him a shepherd's milk; in the cave the Prophet said Allah was their third.
Abu Bakr grasped the Prophet was the slave given a choice; the Prophet would have taken him as Khalil, kept only his gate open, and sent a woman to him.
The Prophet defended Abu Bakr, loved him most of men, dreamt of him drawing water, cleared his slack robe of pride, and hoped all Paradise's gates would call him.
Umar denies the Prophet's death until Abu Bakr recites verses on it; at Bani Saida the people pledge allegiance to Abu Bakr, and Aisha says both speeches benefited them.
Ali names Abu Bakr then Umar as best after the Prophet; Abu Bakr scolds Aisha when her lost necklace halts the people, and the Tayammum verse is revealed.
The Prophet forbids abusing his companions, gives Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman glad tidings of Paradise, and dreams of Abu Bakr and Umar drawing water; Ali prays for Umar.
Asked the worst thing the pagans did to the Prophet, Abdullah bin Amr recalls Uqba throttling him at prayer until Abu Bakr pulled Uqba away.
In dreams the Prophet sees Umar's palace in Paradise and gives him milk meaning knowledge; Satan avoids Umar's path, Muslims grew powerful once he embraced Islam, and Ali praises him.
The Prophet says if any of his followers is inspired it is Umar and interprets Umar's long shirt in a dream as religion; stabbed, Umar fears Allah's punishment.
Uthman gets glad tidings of Paradise along with a calamity and has Al-Walid flogged; he is ranked after Abu Bakr and Umar, and Ibn Umar answers charges against him.
Umar checks Iraq's land tax, is stabbed leading prayer, asks Aisha to be buried beside his two companions and names six for the succession, who settle on Uthman.
Ali gets the flag at Khaybar, is nicknamed Abu Turab and is to the Prophet as Aaron to Moses; he and Fatima are taught bedtime glorifications instead of a servant.
Abu Huraira, often hungry beside the Prophet, calls Ja'far bin Abi Talib the most generous to the poor; Ibn Umar greets Ja'far's son as son of the two-winged one.
In drought Umar asks Allah for rain through the Prophet's uncle Al-Abbas, as they once asked through the Prophet, and rain is given.
Abu Bakr tells Fatima prophets leave charity, not inheritance, but vows kindness to the Prophet's relatives; the Prophet calls Fatima part of him, first of his family to follow him.
Uthman calls Az-Zubair the best and dearest to the Prophet, who names him his disciple and praises his scouting of Bani Quraiza; Az-Zubair is wounded charging at Al-Yarmuk.
Only Talha and Sa'd stayed by the Prophet in a battle; Talha's hand was paralysed shielding him, and Sa'd calls himself an early convert and first Arab archer for Allah.
When Ali seeks to marry Abu Jahl's daughter, the Prophet says Fatima is part of him and praises his truthful son-in-law Abu Al-As, and Ali drops the engagement.
The Prophet defends Usama's and Zaid's command; Usama alone dares intercede for a Makhzumi woman thief, and the Prophet says he would cut even Fatima's hand for theft.
Ibn Umar says the Prophet would have loved Usama's son and Al-Hajjaj, of Um Aiman's family, after making Al-Hajjaj repeat a faulty prayer; the Prophet asked Allah to love Usama.
Ibn Umar dreams angels take him to the Fire; the Prophet says Abdullah would be excellent if he prayed at night, and calls him a pious man.
Abu Ad-Darda praises Kufa's companions Ibn Mas'ud, Ammar and Hudhaifa and confirms Ibn Mas'ud's reading of 'By the Night'; the Prophet calls Abu Ubaida this nation's most trustworthy man.
The Prophet calls Al-Hasan a chief who may reconcile two Muslim groups and asks Allah to love him; Al-Hasan and Al-Husain, who resembled him, are his two sweet basils.
Umar calls Bilal their chief, freed by Abu Bakr; the Prophet prays that Ibn Abbas be taught wisdom, and announces three flag-bearers martyred before Khalid takes the flag to victory.
The Prophet names Ibn Mas'ud first of four to learn the Quran from; Abu Ad-Darda confirms his reading, and Hudhaifa finds him most like the Prophet in conduct.
Ibn Abbas defends Mu'awiya's single-rak'a witr, as he was a companion and a learned man, and Mu'awiya says the Prophet forbade two rak'as after Asr.
The Prophet says Fatima is part of him, and whoever angers her angers him.
Gabriel greets Aisha; her superiority over women is like tharid over food, Ammar calls her the Prophet's wife in both worlds, and revelation came under no wife's blanket but hers.
Allah named the Ansar and brought about the day of Bu'ath so they would embrace Islam; answering their complaint over booty, the Prophet says he would take the Ansar's valley.
The Prophet makes Abdur-Rahman and Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi brothers; Sa'd offers half his property and to divorce a wife for him to marry, but Abdur-Rahman goes to the market instead.
Love of the Ansar is a sign of faith, hatred of hypocrisy; the Prophet calls them among his most beloved, prays their followers count as Ansar, and ranks their families.
The Prophet tells the Ansar to be patient when others are preferred after him until they meet him at the Tank, and prays for the Ansar and Emigrants.
An Ansari couple go hungry to feed the Prophet's guest and a verse is revealed; the Prophet asks rulers to accept the Ansar's good and excuse their wrongdoers.
Sa'd bin Mu'adh's handkerchiefs in Paradise surpass silk and the Throne shook at his death; he judges that Bani Quraiza's warriors be killed and their women and children taken captive.
Two men leaving the Prophet on a very dark night find a light before them, which divides to go with each when they part.
The Prophet names four to learn the Quran from, ranks the Ansar houses and recites to Ubai at Allah's order; Anas says four Ansar collected the Quran.
At Uhud, as the people flee, Abu Talha shields the Prophet and shoots for him, while Aisha and Um Sulaim carry water to the thirsty.
The Prophet calls Abdullah bin Salam a man of Paradise and reads his dream of a pillar as dying a Muslim; Abdullah warns that a debtor's gift is Riba.
Aisha is jealous of Khadija, whom the Prophet often mentions, sending meat to her friends; Khadija and Mary are the best of women, and Khadija is promised a Paradise palace.
The Prophet always smiles at Jarir bin Abdullah, who at his request destroys the pre-Islamic house of Dhul-Khalasa with 150 Ahmas horsemen, killing those found there, and is blessed.
At Uhud, after the pagans' defeat, Satan's shout makes Muslim ranks fight each other, killing Hudhaifa's father despite his son's cries, and Hudhaifa asks Allah to forgive them.
Hind bint Utba, who once wished the Prophet's family degraded, now wishes it honoured; he lets her feed her children from miserly Abu Sufyan's property only what is reasonable.
Before Islam, Zaid bin Amr bin Nufail refuses meat slaughtered for idols, turns from Jewish and Christian scholars to Abraham's religion, and saves little girls from being killed.
Carrying stones to rebuild the Ka'bah, the Prophet falls unconscious on removing his waist sheet; there was no wall around the Ka'bah until Umar built one, raised by Ibn Az-Zubair.
Before Islam people fasted Ashura, shunned Umrah in the Hajj months, swore by their fathers, stood for funerals and left Muzdalifa after sunrise; the Prophet kept or changed some.
The Prophet praises a verse of Labid and forbids selling an unborn camel's offspring; Abu Bakr vomits food earned by fortune-telling, and Abu Talib settles a killing by Qasama.
Inspired at forty, the Prophet in Mecca tells the persecuted Khabbab earlier believers endured worse; Uqba lays entrails on him and throttles him, and the first converts were few.
A tree told the Prophet of the jinn who heard the Quran; he tells Abu Huraira not to bring bones or dung for cleaning, as they are the jinn's food.
Abu Dhar sends his brother to Mecca, then comes himself, is led to the Prophet by Ali, embraces Islam, and is beaten for proclaiming it until Al-Abbas rescues him.
Before his Islam Umar tied Sa'id bin Zaid to make him leave Islam; when Umar converts, Al-As bin Wail protects him from the crowd, and Umar questions a former foreteller.
When the Meccans ask for a miracle, the moon splits in two with Hira between the halves, and at Mina the Prophet tells those with him to bear witness.
Urged to punish his brother Al-Walid, Uthman recalls his two migrations and loyalty to the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar, and has Al-Walid flogged forty lashes.
On the emigrants to Ethiopia: the Prophet condemns pictures and worship places over graves seen there, no longer answers greetings in prayer, and gives the ship's people two migrations.
The Prophet announces the Negus's death the day he dies, calls him a pious man and a brother, and leads his funeral prayer in rows with four Takbir.
Setting out for Hunain, the Prophet plans to camp at Khaif Bani Kinana, where the pagans swore to boycott Banu Hashim.
Dying, Abu Talib holds to Abdul Muttalib's religion; a verse forbids seeking forgiveness for pagans, and the Prophet says thanks to him Abu Talib is in a shallow fire.
When Quraysh disbelieve him, Allah shows the Prophet Jerusalem to describe; he recounts his heart washed, the Buraq, prophets in seven heavens and fifty prayers reduced to five.
Ka'b bin Malik, Jabir and his uncles attended the Aqaba pledge, where, Ubada says, they pledged to worship Allah alone and avoid theft, illegal sexual intercourse, killing and slander.
Aisha tells of being engaged to the Prophet at six and handed to him at nine in Medina; he twice saw her pictured on silk in a dream.
Khabbab says the emigrants' reward is with Allah, recalling Mus'ab's short shroud; emigration counts by intention, ended with Mecca's conquest, and the Prophet lived ten years as an emigrant.
The Prophet tells of a slave choosing what is with Allah over this world; Abu Bakr weeps, is praised for his companionship and wealth, and only his door stays open.
Abu Bakr gives up Ibn ad-Daghina's protection and migrates with the Prophet via Thaur's cave; Suraqa's horse sinks; Asma's son is born at Quba; Abdullah bin Salam accepts Islam.
Umar's grants to early Emigrants; Khabbab on Emigrants who died unrewarded in this world, like Mus'ab; Umar's hope for their deeds with the Prophet; Ibn Umar pledging before his father.
Abu Bakr recounts the journey, milk from a shepherd and hiding in the cave; he kisses feverish Aisha, dyes his hair, divorces Um Bakr; a bedouin asks about migrating.
The first Emigrants and the Prophet reach Medina; he prays for its love and health; Uthman's two migrations; Medina, place of migration and Sunna; Ansar lodge Emigrants by lot.
The day of Bu'ath before the mission divided the tribes and killed their nobles, easing their conversion; girls sing Ansar songs of Bu'ath on Eid, and the Prophet allows it.
The Prophet's mosque is built; Emigrants get three days in Mecca after Hajj; his arrival starts the calendar; prayer becomes four rak'at except travelling; he prays their migration be fulfilled.
The Prophet makes Abdur-Rahman bin Auf and Sa'd bin ar-Rabi' brothers; Abdur-Rahman declines half Sa'd's property, trades, marries an Ansari woman and is told to give a banquet.
Abdullah bin Salam asks the Prophet three things only a prophet can answer, accepts Islam, and the Jews who praised him call him the most wicked among them.
Al-Bara and Zaid bin Arqam say the Prophet allowed selling dirhams hand to hand but not on credit.
The Prophet says had ten Jews believed, all would have; he orders fasting Ashura as they did, wears his hair loose like them, then parts it; they divided the Scripture.
Salman al-Farisi says he was sold from master to master more than ten times, comes from Ram-Hurmuz, and puts six hundred years between Jesus and Muhammad.
Zaid bin Arqam says the Prophet made nineteen expeditions, seventeen of them with him, the first being al-Ashira.
Warned by Sa'd, Umaiya bin Khalaf is urged out by Abu Jahl and killed at Badr; Ka'b missed Badr unblamed; al-Miqdad pledges to fight; the Prophet appeals to Allah.
Al-Bara and Ibn Umar were too young for Badr, whose warriors numbered over three hundred and ten, like the believers who crossed the river with Saul.
The Prophet invokes evil on Quraysh leaders, later seen dead; Ibn Mas'ud finds Abu Jahl dying, struck down by the two sons of Afra, and hears his last words.
The verse on two disputing opponents came down about six who fought at Badr: Hamza, Ali, Ubaida, Shaiba, Utba and al-Walid; Ali duelled in two armours.
Umaiya and his son die at Badr; an old man who would not prostrate is later killed as a disbeliever; Az-Zubair's Badr and Yarmuk wounds and his dented, silver-decorated sword.
The Prophet addresses the Quraysh dead thrown into a Badr well, saying they hear him; Aisha says his words were that they now know, and Ibn Abbas explains verse 14:28.
Haritha, martyred at Badr, is in Firdaus; Hatib, a Badr warrior, is spared over his letter; arrows are used sparingly; Badr and Uhud losses; Afra's sons knock down Abu Jahl.
Ten scouts under Asim bin Thabit are surrounded by Banu Lihyan; Asim falls, Khubaib, sold in Mecca, prays two rak'at before he is killed, and wasps guard Asim's body.
Badr's warriors and angels are ranked the best; Gabriel came armed; Badr men in other reports: a widow's remarriage after childbirth, sacrifice meat after three days, Az-Zubair's spear.
Reports naming Badr warriors: Ubada's pledge, Abu Hudhaifa adopting Salim, a wedding lament for a Badr father, angels avoiding dogs and pictures, drunk Hamza maiming Ali's camels, Hafsa's remarriage.

Reports naming Badr warriors: spending on family as charity, Gabriel offering five prayers at fixed hours, al-Baqara's last two verses, renting fields, Bahrain's jizya, fear of wealth, sparing house snakes.
Abbas's ransom is not waived; a foe professing Islam must be spared; Abu Jahl dies; Badr warriors' stipends and booty shares; the first civil strife leaves none of them alive.
Both tribes fight; Bani An-Nadir are exiled; when Bani Quraiza fight again their men are killed, their women, children and property shared out; al-Hashr is Surat an-Nadir; An-Nadir's palms burnt.
Asked to judge Ali and Abbas over Bani An-Nadir's fai, Umar cites the Prophet: prophets' property is not inherited but given in charity; Abu Bakr answers Fatima and Abbas likewise.
The Prophet asks who will kill Ka'b bin al-Ashraf; Muhammad bin Maslama does so by a ruse; Abdullah bin Atik enters Abu Rafi's castle at night and kills him.
Gabriel comes armed at Uhud; years later the Prophet prays over its martyrs and fears worldly rivalry; archers leave their post for booty, seventy fall, and Abu Sufyan taunts them.
Abdur-Rahman and Khabbab recall Mus'ab's short shroud; promised Paradise, a man drops his dates and fights till martyred; Anas bin an-Nadr's over eighty wounds; verse 33:23 on keeping the covenant.
Verses on the split over those who turned back at Uhud and two clans that nearly faltered; Jabir, his father martyred there, marries a matron; the father's debt is paid.
At Uhud two men in white fight for the Prophet; Sa'd shoots, honoured with 'my father and mother'; Talha and Sa'd alone remain; Abu Talha shields him; women carry water.
At Satan's cry Muslims turn on each other, killing Hudhaifa's father; Ibn Umar says Allah forgave Uthman's flight; the archers retreat, the Apostle calling them back; slumber overtakes Abu Talha.
The Prophet curses certain men, among them Safwan bin Umaiya, Suhail bin Amr and al-Harith bin Hisham, in the morning prayer, and then the verse 'Not for you' comes down.
Um Salit carried water skins at Uhud; Wahshi tells how he speared Hamza and later Musailamah; Allah's wrath on those who wounded the Prophet; Fatima stops his bleeding with ashes.
Seventy go after the pagans following Uhud; the Ansar lost seventy martyrs there; Uhud's dead are buried unwashed, two to a sheet; the Prophet's dream of a broken sword.
Mus'ab's short shroud; the Prophet calls Uhud a mountain that loves us and makes Medina a sanctuary as Abraham did Mecca; he prays over Uhud's martyrs and fears worldly rivalry.
Asim bin Thabit's scouts are surrounded; Asim falls, Khubaib, sold in Mecca, prays two rak'at before Abu Sirwa' kills him, and wasps guard Asim's body.
Seventy reciters are treacherously killed at Bir Ma'una, including Haram and Amir bin Fuhaira; a later-cancelled verse speaks for them; the Prophet says Qunut against the tribes for a month.
Emigrants and Ansar dig the trench hungry as the Prophet carries earth and asks Allah's forgiveness for them; Jabir's meal feeds a thousand, and Ibn Umar fights aged fifteen.
When people differ over the caliphate and Muawiya claims a greater right to it, Ibn Umar holds back his reply for fear of causing division and bloodshed.
The Prophet says Muslims will now attack the clans, not be attacked; Asr is delayed past sunset, Az-Zubair is called his disciple, and Allah alone defeated the clans.
Gabriel sends the Prophet against Banu Qurayzah, whom Sa'd bin Mu'adh judges: warriors killed, offspring captive; Sa'd dies of his wound, and Hassan is told to abuse them in verse.
On the Dhat-ur-Riqa and Najd expeditions the Prophet leads the Fear Prayer with two batches in turn, and spares a bedouin who seized his sword as he slept.
On the Banu al-Mustaliq expedition men holding Arab captives ask about coitus interruptus; the Prophet says it is better not to, for every soul destined to exist will exist.
On the Najd expedition a bedouin draws the sleeping Prophet's sword and asks who will save him; the Prophet says 'Allah', and does not punish him.
During the Anmar expedition the Prophet offers voluntary prayers on his mount, facing east.
Aisha tells how, left behind by the army, she was slandered until revelation declared her innocent; further reports concern Ali's silence, her fainting at the news, and Hassan's part.
One rainy night in the year of al-Hudaybiya, the Prophet relays Allah's word: whoever credits rain to Allah's mercy believes in Him, and whoever credits a star disbelieves in Him.
The Prophet's four Umrahs include al-Hudaybiya, where a dried well refills and water flows from his fingers for the 1300 to 1500 men whose pledge al-Bara calls the true victory.
A report from Mirdas al-Aslami, who pledged under the Tree: the pious will pass away one after another, leaving worthless dregs to whom Allah pays no attention.
Setting out with 1300 to 1500 companions, the Prophet takes Ihram; Ka'b shaves his lice-ridden head for a ransom, Umar provides for a pledger's daughter, and the Tree is forgotten.
Pledgers under the Tree say they pledged for death, the pledge verse 48:1 refers to, and report the Prophet on charity, Friday prayer and donkey meat; one rules on witr.
Marching for Umrah, the Prophet consults on Quraysh barring him and accepts Suhail's term to return their men; emigrant women are tested, and the 'manifest victory' sura is revealed.
If barred from the Ka'bah, Ibn Umar will do as the Prophet did when Quraysh barred him, sacrifice and shave; he pledged under the Tree before Umar did.
When the Prophet performs Umrah, making Tawaf, praying and going between Safa and Marwa, his companions guard him against the people of Mecca.
Back from Siffin, Sahl bin Hunaif recalls wanting to refuse the Prophet's order on the day of Abu Jandal; lice-ridden Ka'b is told to shave and pay a ransom.
People of Ukl and Uraina accept Islam, then revert, kill the Prophet's shepherd and drive off the camels; caught, their eyes are branded and hands and legs cut off.
Salama bin al-Akwa chases the Ghatafan raiders who seized the Prophet's camels at Dhi-Qarad, recovers them with his arrows, and is told by the Prophet to forgive them.
At Khaibar, Amir bin al-Akwa dies by his own blade yet earns a double reward; the Prophet attacks at dawn, forbids donkey meat, and frees and marries the captive Safiya.
A fierce fighter the Prophet says is of Hell kills himself; the Prophet bids the army lower their voices, heals Salama's wound, and gives Ali the flag for Khaibar's conquest.
Returning from Khaibar, the Prophet marries Safiya, holds a wedding feast without meat or bread, and veils her, marking her as one of his wives rather than a slave.
At Khaibar the Prophet forbids donkey meat, as well as garlic and temporary marriage, has the pots overturned and allows horse meat; companions differ over the reason for the ban.
Khaibar's booty gives a horseman three shares and a foot soldier one; Banu al-Muttalib, called one with Banu Hashim, get part of its fifth, but Abd Shams and Nawfal none.
Abu Musa's party, whose boat took them to Ethiopia, reach the Prophet at Khaibar; he credits them with two migrations to Umar's one and knows the Ash'aris by their recitation.
Khaibar's booty: Abu Musa's late party get a share but Aban's none, a sheet stolen before division burns its taker, and Umar keeps conquered land undivided for all Muslims.
Abu Bakr refuses Fatima the Prophet's property, which the Prophet said is charity, not inheritance; after her death Ali, aggrieved at not being consulted, pledges allegiance to him.
Khaibar's governor must not swap poor dates for fewer fine ones; its Jews farm it for half the crop, Muslims finally eat their fill, and a poisoned sheep is presented.
When people criticise Usama bin Zaid's command, the Prophet says they once criticised his father's, who was fit to command and dear to him, as Usama now is.
Under the treaty the Prophet returns next year for a three-day Umrah, Muslims walking briskly to show strength; Hamza's daughter is given to her aunt, and he marries Maimuna.
At Mu'tah, Zaid, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha lead in turn and are martyred, Ja'far wounded only in front; the Prophet weeps, forbids the women's crying, and Khalid breaks nine swords.
Usama kills a man at al-Huraqa who had said there is no god but Allah; the Prophet's repeated rebuke makes Usama wish he had embraced Islam only that day.
Salama bin al-Akwa counts seven or nine expeditions with the Prophet, including Khaibar, al-Hudaybiya, Hunain and al-Qarad, and more under commanders such as Abu Bakr and Usama.
Hatib's letter telling Mecca's pagans the Prophet's plans is intercepted; the Prophet accepts his excuse and spares him as a Badr veteran, and a verse forbids befriending Allah's enemies.
In Ramadan of the Conquest year the Prophet sets out fasting with ten thousand men, then breaks his fast publicly on the way, so travellers may fast or not.
Abu Sufyan, caught near Mecca, accepts Islam and watches the army pass; the Prophet recites Surat al-Fath on his camel, notes Aqil left no house, and orders Ibn Khatal killed.
Entering Mecca by Kada, the Prophet strikes the 360 idols round the Ka'bah, has its images removed before entering it, and prays eight rak'at of Duha at Umm Hani's.
In his bowings and prostrations the Prophet used to glorify and praise Allah, our Lord, and ask Him for forgiveness.
Umar asks the Badr elders and Ibn Abbas about the sura on Allah's help and the conquest; Ibn Abbas says it signals the Prophet's approaching death, and Umar agrees.
On the second day of the Conquest the Prophet declares Mecca a sanctuary from Allah where no blood may be shed nor trees cut, fighting allowed him only briefly.
In Mecca in the Conquest year the Prophet declares that Allah and His Messenger have made the selling of wine unlawful.
Staying in Mecca for ten or nineteen days, the Prophet and his companions shorten their prayers; Ibn Abbas shortens up to nineteen days and prays in full beyond.
Amr bin Salama recalls tribes awaiting the Conquest to embrace Islam and his leading their prayer as a boy who knew most Quran; two others met the Prophet that year.
At the Conquest the Prophet rules Zam'a's slave-girl's son, claimed for Utba, is Abd bin Zam'a's brother, for the child belongs to the bed, but has Sauda veil from him.
During the Conquest a woman steals; rejecting Usama's plea, the Prophet says he would cut even Fatima's hand, and hers is cut; she sincerely repents and later marries.
After the Conquest the Prophet takes pledges for Islam and jihad, not migration; Ibn Umar and Aisha say migration has ended, though jihad and intention remain, as Islam now prevails.
On the day of the Conquest the Prophet declares Mecca a sanctuary until the Day of Resurrection, where game is not chased nor plants cut, except idhkhir at al-Abbas's request.
Ibn Abi Aufa bears a Hunain scar; al-Bara says that when Hawazin's arrows routed the hasty, the Prophet did not flee but proclaimed himself the Prophet, son of Abdul-Muttalib.
When Hawazin's delegation, now Muslim, asks back their property and captives, the Prophet has them choose one, and the Muslims willingly return the captives, as their chiefs confirm.
Returning from Hunain, Umar asks about his pre-Islamic vow to perform I'tikaf, and the Prophet tells him to fulfil it.
At Hunain Abu Qatada gets the spoils of a pagan he killed; after Hunain Abu Amir is shot at Autas, and the Prophet asks forgiveness for him and Abu Musa.
While besieging Ta'if the Prophet bars an effeminate man from entering upon women; when the fort holds out, his companions fight and are wounded, then gladly agree to return.
Sa'd, first to shoot an arrow in Allah's cause, and Abu Bakra, who came over Ta'if's fort wall, report that knowingly claiming a false father denies one Paradise.
At al-Ji'rana a bedouin rejects the Prophet's good tidings, so Abu Musa and Bilal accept them and drink and pour on themselves water he had washed in.
At al-Ji'rana Ya'la sees the Prophet red-faced under revelation, after which he tells a man in Ihram for Umrah to wash off his perfume and remove his cloak.
The Prophet gives Hunain's booty to Quraish and new Muslims, not the Ansar, asking them to be content to take him home; faulted by a man, he recalls Moses' patience.
A detachment sent to Najd returns with thirteen camels each; Khalid kills and captures men of Jadhima who said 'Saba'na' instead of 'Aslamna', and the Prophet disowns what Khalid did.
An angry commander orders his troops into a fire; they hold back, and the Prophet says they would never have come out, obedience being due only in what is good.
